# 4 Cooperative Transport Interface (CTI)

## 4.1 General Network Architecture and Mechanism
With reference to the O-RAN CUS [2] and O-RAN MP [3] specifications, the fronthaul reference architecture is extended to include the cooperative transport interface and transport network, as depicted in Figure 4.1, where the new functions are defined as follows:

# 7 Figure 4.1 : CTI basic reference architecture
Cooperative Transport Interface (CTI): an O-RAN defined interface designed to support real-time and non-real time cooperation between the eNB/gNB and the resource allocation based transport networks. Transport Network: transfers lls-C/U/S and lls-M traffics between O-DU and O-RU. Transport Node (TN): a master transport network node at O-DU side. A TN schedules one or multiple TUs to perform resource allocation for upstream transmission. It also interfaces with O-DU via CTI and decodes T-plane messages in order to coordinate its own scheduling with forward-looking traffic requirements communicated by O-DU. Transport Unit (TU): a slave transport network node at O-RU side. The control and management interface between TN and TU is out of scope of this document. CTI TC-plane: (Transport Control plane). The TC-plane refers specifically to real-time Transport Control between the CTI Client in the O-DU and the CTI Server in the TN.. CTI TM (Transport Management). The TM Information Model / Data Model model refers to the configuration of parameters for the CTI functionality on the O-DU, and to those CTI configuration parameters that need to be coordinated between mobile SMO and transport network OSS. The purpose of CTI (TC-plane and TM model) is to support cooperation between the O-DU and the TN in the transport network. The interface between TN and TU is transport network specific and is out of the scope of this specification. Figure 4.2 shows how the CTI relates to the transport network used for fronthaul. The uplink latency T34max is specified between the R3 reference point of the O-RU and the R4 reference point of the O-DU. Note that additionally there could be intermediate nodes (switches or routers) between the O-DUs and TNs (not shown in the figure). These nodes do not interact with the CTI process. However, they can introduce extra latency, which need then to be subtracted from the T34max limit to obtain the resulting latency budget for the TN-TU part of the transport network.

# 8 Figure 4.2 : Detailed view of CTI

### 4.1.1 High Level CTI Message Flow
Figure 4.3 below illustrates a high level view of how CTI works. For simplification only a single O-RU and a single O- DU are shown. The UEs are not shown in this figure. Figure 4.3 : Message Flow for CTI in UL Operations The actions and related message exchanges are as follows:

# 19 1. O-DU determines UE grants for slot n.
2. O-DU sends the CTI message to the TN to request fronthaul bytes for slot n, sufficiently in advance (see Figure

### 4.1.2 Packet-based Transport Network topologies supported by CTI
The simplest way to provide connectivity for Fronthaul is to provide one point-point link (e.g. optical fiber) between each O-RU network interface and its correspodning O-DU. One O-DU can serve multiple O-RUs, and each O-RU can have multiple network interfaces and multiple radio carriers (which may also be known as cells). The upstream radio traffic in the radio carriers is scheduled by O-DU schedulers. In such case there is no sharing of transport resources, each connection has its dedicated bandwidth and physical link, the CTI mechanism is not required. Figure 4.4 : Direct interconnections between multiple O-DUs and multiple O-RUs over point-point links Things change when a packet-based transport network is used to interconnect the O-DUs and their corresponding O-RUs. The use of CTI targets transport networks that contain Transport Nodes (TNs) that terminate one or multiple shared distribution networks, where each distribution network (one port on one TN) aggregates multiple Transport Units (TUs). This implies that the bandwidth of a distribution network is shared among multiple TUs. In the upstream direction, the TN manages this sharing by scheduling bandwidth allocations to the multiple TUs. The concept of CTI can be applied to inform the relevant Transport Nodes (TN) of the required uplink traffic load and traffic timing that each O-RU to O-DU connection will have to carry. There is a need to uniquely indentify the corresponding connection in each traffic request being signaled over CTI. This identifier is added by the O-DU, and shall be commonly known by both the O-DU and TN. However, the identifier should be agnostic of any TN-technology- specific parameters in order to maintain general applicability of the concept to any technology. The TN then has the responsibility to translate this generic identifier into its own technology-specific parameters, e,g. a Transmission Container (T-CONT) or Logical Link ID (LLID) for PON (the TN being an OLT) or a Service Flow (SF) for DOCSIS

# 8 (the TN being a CMTS).
The uniqueness of the identifier shall allow for multiple architecture use cases, whereby the O-DU should not be dependent on the underlying Transport Network topology. The different architecture use cases are illustrated in Figure 4.5. Basically, O-DUs and TNs may be connected in multiple ways (each O-DU may connect to multiple TNs, each TN may connect to multiple O-DUs). Figure 4.5 : Possible interconnections between multiple O-DUs and multiple O-RUs over a transport network consisting of a multitude of Transport Nodes (TNs) and their corresponding shared distribution networks with multiple Transport Units (TUs). Basically, a “fronthaul traffic flow” is a flow of packets that requires a given capacity and latency limit. A unique identification is needed in the TN to convert a request for a fronthaul traffic flow into a scheduling action on the corresponding managed entity (Traffic Container / alloc-ID or Logical Link ID in PON or Service Flow in DOCSIS) on the corresponding TU (PON ONU or DOCSIS CM). The unique identification consists of two parts. The first is called “CTI Session ID” and refers uniquely and globally to a specific O-RU physical interface (used by one or multiple radio carriers). In case there is no differentiation beyond the O-RU physical interface, the CTI Session ID is sufficient. The second is called “Flow ID”, which allows to differentiate and report different fronthaul flows per CTI session. The CTI Flow ID is unique only within the context of its CTI Session ID, the same CTI Flow IDs may be re-used across different sessions. See section 5 for more details. Examples of using the CTI Session ID and CTI Flow ID are shown in Figure 4.5:  O-RU 1: 1:1 mapping between one O-DU scheduler and one O-RU interface (single radio carrier instance), carrying a single flow. A single CTI Session ID is sufficient. A single report is communicated.  O-RU 2: 1:1 mapping between one O-DU scheduler and one O-RU interface (single radio carrier instance), carrying multiple flows. A single CTI Session ID is sufficient. Multiple reports with different Flow IDs may be used to differentiate the flows.  O-RU 3 and O-RU 4: Multiple O-RUs being served by a single TU, each with 1:1 mappings between an O-DU scheduler and an O-RU interface. Each O-RU has one different CTI session ID.  O-RU 5: N:1 mapping between multiple radio carrier instances (e.g. multiple sectors, multiple frequency bands) and one O-RU interface. A single message may be used, with a single CTI Session ID reporting the sum of the different radio carrier loads. Alternatively, multiple messages (from a single or from multiple CTI clients) may also be used, which are then interpreted together by the TN.  O-RU 6: Multiple 1:1 mappings between one O-DU scheduler and one O-RU interface, on the same O-RU and TU. One CTI Session ID is used per O-RU interface.

# 7 Notes
 These high-level use cases may also be combined together (e.g. Multiple flows on multiple O-RU interfaces).

# 9 The protocol also supports such combined use cases.
 The use case of multiple network interfaces per radio carrier (for bonding or redundancy purposes) is out of scope of this version on CTI. This specification only considers a single network interface per radio carrier. In case of multiple radio carriers, it is assumed in this specification that each uses a single O-RU network interface (which could be the same as the other radio instances, or a dedicated one (like O-RU 6 in Figure 2-5).  The CTI client side generating the CTI reports may be implemented as multiple instances per O-DU.  The CTI server side treating the CTI reports may be implemented as multiple instances per TN. There are two possible ways to populate the CTI Session IDs in the O-DUs and TNs, either statically by means of preconfiguration via their OAM systems, or dynamically by means of an auto-discovery mechanism (see section 5.2.1). The CTI operation between the O-DU and the TN is specified independently of the configuration method of the CTI

# 19 Session IDs.

### 4.1.3 Forwarding and addressing of CTI messages
The CTI messages generated by a CTI instance in the O-DU shall be forwarded to and addressed to the corresponding CTI peer in the corresponding TN. Depending on the interconnection between the O-DUs and the TNs, CTI messages are encapsulated at Layer 2 or at Layer 3:  Point to point links; Layer 2 or Layer 3

# 25  Ethernet switches; Layer 2 or Layer 3

# 26  IP Routers; Layer 3

# 27 Encapsulation details are described in section 5.1.

## 4.2 Information Required for Cooperative Transport

### 4.2.1 From O-DU to Transport
The O-DU needs to convey the bandwidth needs per O-RU interface per time interval with a unique identifier of the traffic being reported. There is also the option to convey information about load patterns inside the reported time interval.

# 32 A report carries the following information;
 Time interval End (time at which all fronthaul packets pertaining to that time interval have been sent by the O-

# 34 RU)
 Time interval Start (time at which fronthaul packets pertaining to that time interval start to be sent by the O-RU)

# 36  CTI Session ID + optionally Flow ID
 Required load for the time interval of the session (and flow in the session) The TN needs to correlate the unique identification (CTI Session ID + optionally Flow ID) to a corresponding unique traffic container on a corresponding TU. The TN needs to interpret the required load and convert it to bandwidth allocations corresponding to the reported time interval. The TN should also be aware of the latency budget it has available per O-RU interface (or per flow per O-RU interface in case of differentiation between multiple flows). This is the portion of T34max for the TN-TU segment. It allows the TN to give relative priorities between the fronthaul connections it manages. As this parameter is a fixed value, it is not carried in CTI messages but should be configured on the TN by its OAM.

### 4.2.2 From Transport to O-DU
Uplink CTI messages may be used for the specific case of notification of PON ranging (see Annex A.1.4 for background on PON ranging). The uplink interruptions caused by PON ranging will be felt in the O-DU as jitter or packet drop on the upstream fronthaul packets. In worst case, the interruptions can be in the order of several hundreds of µs. Such relatively short interruptions will not cause an outage of the radio system (no action by the network, no radio link interruption), but can still have detrimental effects, depending on whether the data is protected by HARQ and on the way the O-DU would react to the perceived jitter or loss. However, an adaptive RAN scheduler might conclude the degradation is due to an impaired radio channel, which would be inappropriate and could lead to wrong reactions by the O-DU, further degrading performance. To avoid this, the O- DU can benefit from knowing when the uplink is subject to interruptions due to the transport network. A specific CTI signaling message is defined in section 5.1.3.1 that allows the TN (OLT) to notify the O-DU about an upcoming ranging event. One event has a maximum duration and contains a series of interruptions. A PON ranging notification carries the following information;  Event start and Maximal Event duration in which ranging interruptions will occur  Maximal duration per interruption (corresponding to the quiet window size on the PON)  List of CTI Session IDs impacted by the ranging event The CTI Server in the TN (OLT) sends a ranging notification for a PON to every CTI Client that manages one or multiple

# 25 CTI sessions on that given PON.
The notification message has to arrive at the O-DU at least 10 ms in advance of the event. The O-DU is free to apply whatever proprietary action after reception of the ranging notifications. Figure 4.6 : Notification of PON ranging upstream interruptions

## 4.3 Calculation of CTI reports by O-DU

### 4.3.1 Required load
Uplink fronthaul traffic from O-RU to O-DU can consist of U-plane, C-plane, and M-plane packets. The load reporting by CTI has to allow the TN to follow the traffic variations over time, but this needs prediction of this traffic.

# 11 Layer 2 and/or Layer 3 mapping.
For cases where one O-RU (or O-RU interface) aggregates fronthaul traffic from multiple RAN schedulers (e.g. multiple sectors), the O-DU shall be able to report the full traffic load for the O-RU (or O-RU interface) in an aggregated message, or in separate messages, and the TN has to interpret all information for the O-RU (or O-RU interface).

# 15 4.3.1.2 C-plane
Uplink C-plane messages are not present except for the special case of Licensed Assisted Access (LAA). If LAA is used, the C-plane uplink traffic consists of messages for Listen Before Talk (LBT). LBT is performed per carrier. There can be more than one carrier per RU. It is expected that typical deployments will be maximum 4 carriers. The LBT process depends on the channel utilization and is hence unpredictable, but it is possible to determine the following worst-case assumptions:
- Repetition of LBT_PDSCH_RSP every subframe (1ms) of (message size 25 Bytes). With max 4 carriers this
gives 4 such messages per subframe.
- Repetition of the other messages LBT_DRS_RSP, LBT_Buffer_Error, LBT_CWCONFIG_RSP (message sizes
of 21 Bytes) is much less, the assumption is one of those messages every subframe (1ms)
- Assuming transport over UDP/IPv4/tagged Ethernet gives encapsulation overhead of 50 Bytes per message
- Full burstiness; the O-RU sends these 5 messages back-to-back close to the end of the subframe, but exact timing
can vary.
- The average C-plane uplink load is 3 Mbit/s per O-RU.
In terms of latency, there are two aspects to take care of. First, the typical latency requirement for LBT C-plane messages themselves is 0.5ms (minus some margin for processing). Second, the presence of uplink C-plane messages may not push the latency of uplink U-plane messages above their tolerance threshold. There are two ways to accommodate for the uplink C-plane messages;

# 35 Including C-plane traffic in CTI messaging
The C-plane may be part of the CTI reporting when the CTI client continuously adds a certain fixed bandwidth (eg based on the above worst-case example) for the C-plane traffic in all its reports. The advantage is that the transport network does not need to be aware of the nature of such traffic and does not need extra configuration, and the O-DU can use a simple constant term in its calculations. Such allocated bandwidth for C-plane messages shall ensure that they are not buffered too long, so that their latency is respected (assuming 0.45ms for including processing time). In the example above this requires to include enough extra bandwidth in each report to transmit 3 Mbit/s in less than 0.45ms, being an extra bandwidth of at least 6.6 Mbit/s. (Because the exact timing of the LBT messages is not known, even if the CTI reporting would be more frequent than the frequency of LBT messages (1ms), it would not be accurate to estimate which report would be capturing the LBT messages, so the extra bandwidth shall be granted in each report). The impact of C-plane on U-plane latency is due to the sharing of the same TU buffer for U-plane and C-plane packets, and the TDM nature of the transport network (bandwidth allocation is not (fully) done by line rate adjustment but (also) by TDM burst adjustment). C-plane packets in the head of the queue will impact U-plane packets behind them. U-plane traffic typically has stricter transport latency requirements than the 0.5ms (or 0.45ms) for the C-plane traffic.
- If the U-plane bandwidth gets small compared to the C-plane bandwidth and the combined allocated bandwidth
is just their sum, then the C-plane packets could block the U-plane packets behind them for too long before being transmitted. Hence a floor value of allocated bandwidth (even if U-plane traffic would be very low) could be needed.
- Most of the time the U-plane traffic is much higher than the C-plane traffic, but even so if the allocated bandwidth
is just the sum of C- and U-plane traffic, the U-plane traffic could need more TDM bursts to be fully transmitted than without the C-plane traffic. This increases latency. Using a higher value than the actual C-plane traffic as the extra term in the CTI report calculation could be needed to reduce this impact. This has to be estimated depending on the technology of the Transport network and the latency requirements. In summary, this approach may be chosen by configuring at the CTI client (per CTI session ID) a parameter for a fixed extra bandwidth (#bytes to be added per report) and a parameter for a minimum total bandwidth (minimum #bytes to be used per report independently of the actual need). The CTI server and TN is not aware of the differences between U-plane and C-plane. Separate transport flows for uplink C-plane traffic and uplink U-plane traffic Alternatively, for full latency isolation of C-plane and U-plane traffic, the transport system may offer a dedicated and fixed uplink transport channel that can be used for LBT messages. The C-plane packets would have to be uniquely identified for classification to the transport flow (eg by means of PCP or DSCP marking). The C-plane traffic is then decoupled from the CTI reporting, CTI only handles U-plane uplink traffic in CTI-controlled transport channel. The U- plane traffic will not share the same TU buffer and will experience latency impact from the C-plane traffic. The transport system should provide a dedicated bandwidth to the C-plane transport channel that provides sufficiently low latency. This requires the O-RU to be configured to apply differentiated marking between C-plane and U-plane traffic, and coordination between Transport and Mobile management systems to configure an appropriate value of the dedicated C-plane transport channel bandwidth. In CTI messages there is no need to take C-plane traffic into account, so the fixed extra bandwidth and minimum total bandwidth may be set to 0 in the configuration of the CTI client.

# 28 4.3.1.3 M-plane
The M-plane uplink traffic is not fully predictable by the O-DU. However, that traffic is much less latency-sensitive and can be differentiated by different Layer 2 or Layer 3 marking from U-plane and C-plane. It may be kept out of CTI reporting and transported separately from the U-plane and C-plane traffic by the TN.

### 4.3.2 Time interval of the reported load
The TN shall be informed about the time interval in which the reported load will be arriving at the TU interface. Each CTI message can carry the start and end of uplink fronthaul transmission on the O-RU R3 interface (please see section

# 35 5.1.4.2 and 5.1.4.3).
There is an inherent O-RU latency Ta3 between the antenna interface Ra and the uplink reference point R3, characterized by the O-RU category with a margin of 20µs or 50µs (See Table B-5 in O-RAN CUS [2]). The O-DU is aware of the category per O-RU. In CTI a time of day is communicated as a Base time (granularity in ns) + an Offset (granularity in µs), see section 5.1.4.1. Accuracy of time references (Base + Offset) shall be better than half the category margin, namely 10µs (-5µs/+5µs).

### 4.3.3 Exchange rate of CTI Reporting

# 3 1 ms

# 4 0,5 ms

# 5 0,25 ms
When a CTI_MIN value is specified at O-DU level, it means all active CTI clients on the O-DU shall support the rate, e.g. when multiple clients are used for a same Session ID they have to operate at the same message exchange rate. Alternatively CTI_MIN can be specified per CTI client instance. Note that a category only represents a capability, it does NOT mandate the use of that particular value as actual CTI message exchange rate. The selection of the actual rate is described hereunder.

# 19 4.3.3.2 Determining common nominal CTI rate (CTI_NOM)
A common CTI rate shall be selected for a given combination of O-DU and TN and a given mobile slot duration. The common rate is a nominal value for the spacing between two messages, expressed as CTI_NOM. In principle, the maximum CTI exchange rate that is ever needed is one reporting message per mobile slot duration, as this is the granularity at which the RAN schedulers can allocate traffic. But such high exchange rate will not always be possible or even needed. If the common CTI rate is less than once per every mobile slot, multiple mobile slots have to be grouped in the same CTI reporting message, so CTI_NOM shall always follow an integer number (N ≥ 1) of mobile slot units. CTI_NOM shall comply to both of the following:

# 27 1) Shall be supported by O-DU and TN:

# 28 CTI_NOM ≥ max(CTI_MIN(O-RU), CTI_MIN(TN))
2) Shall be a multiple of mobile slot duration: CTI_NOM = N × (mobile slot duration), where N is a non-zero integer, and depends on the latency requirements. Example: Assuming a mobile slot of 0.5ms, if an O-DU supports a CTI_MIN of 0.5ms and a TN supports a CTI_MIN of 1ms, the fastest common CTI exchange rate would be CTI_NOM = 1ms (containing 2 mobile slots). However, if the required latency can still be reached by applying a higher CTI_NOM like 1.5ms (3 mobile slots) or 2ms (4 mobile slots), it is allowed to use such larger values as well.

# 37 CTI_NOM has to be interpreted as follows:
- If no load is to be reported for some period, CTI messages don’t need to be sent at CTI_NOM rate, so the spacing
may be larger. Keepalives are still exchanged periodically in any case. See section 5.2.2 for background.
- CTI_NOM represents an average rate and not a strict message spacing, there may be some jitter on CTI messages
themselves, see section 4.2 for background. The sequence number inside each CTI message can be used to detect the drop of a CTI message. Further actions for missing or out-of-order sequence numbers are not specified in this specification.

# 5 CTI Message Protocol
This section describes the mandatory functions of the CTI protocol. Figure 5.1 is a reference diagram that includes the ORAN system and transport system functional blocks. The transmission system could be a PON or DOCSIS transport system.

# 7 Figure 5.1 : Fronthaul Reference Diagram
The O-RU can have one or more carriers (e.g., multiple antennas, multiple sectors), each corresponding to one eAxC and one RAN scheduler. One RAN scheduler can manage multiple carriers. The O-RU can also have one or more network interfaces between itself and the TU. The O-RU is responsible for associating byte streams from each carrier (antenna/sector) to a unique network interface. The CTI message describes the byte flow across a single network interface. Requirements are only listed for the ORAN components. This document provides the expectation on the transport network. Any parameter quoted as having a value “N” is a variable that is unique per usage. Note that N:1 and N:N in the above figure indicate many to 1, and many to many relations, respectively.

## 5.1 CTI Packet Format
The bit order and Byte order in which all CTI messages are transported shall follow the order shown in Figure 5.2. Figure 5.2 : Order of transmission of CTI messages The O-DU shall support Ethernet II as Layer 2, including the tagging aspects:

# 21  untagged Ethernet

# 22  single tagged (802.1Q) Ethernet

# 23  dual-tagged (802.1ad) Ethernet
Use of Ethernet by the O-DU is mandatory. The choice of tagging is left to the operator. Support of IPv4 as Layer 3 is mandatory in the O-DU. Use of IPv4 or IPv6 by the O-DU is optional. When IPv4 or IPv6 is used, CTI is carried over UDP. The CTI messages are exchanged between the CTI client located in the O-DU and the CTI server located in the TN. A message is either sent from the O-DU to the TN or from the TN to the O-DU. The CTI client and CTI server shall format the CTI messages specified in Figure 5.3 and Table 5.1, Table 5.3, and Table

# 4 5.7.

# 6 Figure 5.3 : CTI Message Format.
The message is either transported over UDP/IP over Ethernet (using IPv4 or IPv6 Ethertype), or directly over

# 8 Ethernet (using O-RAN Ethertype and O-RAN Protocol subtype).
When IP is not used, the fields are (example for 802.1Q):  Ethernet MAC destination address is the MAC address of the CTI message receiver  Ethernet MAC source address is the MAC address of the CTI message sender  802.1Q TPID value 0x8100 which indicates the presence of a VLAN header

# 4  802.1Q PCP is determined by configuration

# 5  802.1Q VLAN ID is determined by configuration
 EtherType has value of 0x9433, dedicated for use by O-RAN.  A 2-byte Protocol subtype. The protocol subtype for CTI is 0x0001. When IP is used, the fields are (example for 802.1Q):  Ethernet MAC destination address is the MAC address of the CTI message receiver corresponding to its IP address (or the interface of the next hop router)  Ethernet MAC source address is the MAC address of the CTI message sender corresponding to its IP address (or the interface of the last hop router)  802.1Q TPID value 0x8100 which indicates the presence of a VLAN header if it is included

# 15  802.1Q PCP is assigned by the operator
 802.1Q VLAN ID is assigned by the operator  EtherType is value 0x0800 (IPv4) or 0x86DD (IPv6)  IPv4 ToS / IPv6 TC is assigned by configuration  IPv4 Protocol Field = UDP ; IPv6 Next Header Field = UDP  the IP source address is the IP address of the sender  the IP destination address is defined by the sender’s OSS System  the UDP source port is defined by the sender’s OSS System, and  the UDP destination port is defined by the sender’s OSS System The contents of the payload (Ethernet or UDP) contain the CTI message elements as described in Table 5.1, followed by an optional CTI Signature, as defined in Section 5.1.5. The optionality of the CTI Signature and how it is configured is for a future release of this specification. For processing simplicity at TN, a CTI message shall not be fragmented over multiple packets or frames. Note that the configuration of L2/L3 parameters for CTI transport is described in O-RAN CTI TMP [4].

### 5.1.1 CTI Message Format

# A CTI message either conveys CTI reports or CTI signaling. In both cases, the message has a common message header.

 One or more mobile slots with a single report entry  More than one mobile slots with multiple report entries  One or more flows within a mobile slot by using multiple report entries  One of more flows across multiple mobile slots by using multiple report entries

# 10 The typical packet length would be as follows.

# 17 5.1.4.2 CTI Type 1 Row
Each Type 1 row represents a report entry and is used to request some number of bytes at some future time on a specific CTI flow. Each CTI row entry includes a CTI Flow ID, the end time offset and the number of bytes requested. The CTI Flow ID is defined via OSS and is common between the TN and the O-DU. The purpose of CTI Type 1 Row is to convey the Requested Bytes (3 bytes in length) associated with a particular Flow ID and end time. The valid range of the Flow ID is 0x00 to 0xEF. The value 0x00 indicates there is no differentiation between the flows and that the Flow ID does not need to be interpreted by the CTI server. The reserved types range from 0xF0 to 0xFD, allowing the option to use 0xFE to 0xFF to indicate special row extension types.

# A CTI Flow corresponds to a flow of packets that can be identified with a set of unique L2 and/or L3 headers that all
traverse the same O-RU network interface and share the same QoS. Typically, there is one CTI Flow ID per fronthaul flow, as designated by the eAxC header in the eCPRI message. CTI may report each fronthaul flow individually. Alternatively, CTI may aggregate multiple fronthaul flows that are traversing the same O-RU network interface into one CTI Flow ID. The CTI message may also have more than one entry per CTI Flow ID. This allows for a lower frequency of CTI messages to still cover multiple traffic intervals of the flow.

# 6 5.1.4.3 CTI Type 1 Extension Row
The purpose of CTI Type 1 Extension Row is to convey the start time offset of the considered time interval and the fronthaul traffic pattern descriptor (encoded as the CTI Pattern ID), as defined in Table 5.7. The CTI client may include one or multiple Type 1 Extension Rows in a CTI message and shall respect following rules:
- A Type 1 Extension Row shall be included directly after a CTI Type 1 Row and such Type 1 Extension Row
then applies to all previous Type 1 Rows until a previous Type 1 Extension Row or the first Type 1 Row in the message.
- The CTI client shall not include more than one CTI Type 1 Extension Row directly following a given CTI Type

# 14 1 Row.
- The CTI client shall not include a CTI Type 1 Extension Row without a CTI Type 1 Row.
Examples of combinations of CTI Type 1 Rows and CTI Type 1 Extension Rows in a CTI report message are illustrated below: flow with 2 patterns Flow ID End time offset Start time offset Pattern ID Bytes requested Type 1 Row 1 k X Type 1 Extension row j A Type 1 Row 1 k Y Type 1 Extension row j B flows with single pattern Flow ID End time offset Start time offset Pattern ID Bytes requested per flow Type 1 Row 1 k X Type 1 Row 2 k Y Type 1 Extension row j A flows with 2 patterns per Flow ID End time offset Start time offset Pattern ID Bytes requested flow Type 1 Row 1 k W Type 1 Extension row j A Type 1 Row 1 k X Type 1 Extension row j B Type 1 Row 2 k Y Type 1 Extension row j C Type 1 Row 2 k Z Type 1 Extension row j D flow with single pattern, Flow ID End time offset Start time offset Pattern ID Bytes requested multiple intervals Type 1 Row 1 k X Type 1 Extension row j A Type 1 Row 1 l Y Type 1 Extension row k A The Extension Field uses a reserved value of 0xFF to indicate that the current row is an extension row for fronthaul. The start time of the CTI Type 1 Extension Row and the End time offset of its corresponding (preceding) CTI Type 1 Row(s) together define an interval (e.g., a mobile slot) whose traffic pattern may be described by the CTI Pattern ID field in the CTI Type 1 Extension Row. See Figure 5.6 for the time offsets. The use of the Pattern ID is optional: the Type 1 Extension Row may also be used to only communicate the start time of the time interval without details of the traffic pattern, by using CTI Pattern ID value of 0.

# 9 5.1.4.4 CTI Type 2 Row
The purpose of CTI Type 2 Row is to allow the measurement of message latency by the TN. The Type 2 Row is optional and if used it shall only be included at the end of the CTI report body, with or without the presence of a CTI Type 1 Row. The CTI client shall not include more than one CTI Type 2 Row per CTI message. The Extension Field uses a reserved value of 0xFE to indicate that the current row is a special row. The CTI message generation time (see Figure 5.6) is useful to calculate the transmission time of a CTI message and the jitter between the CTI messages. The value is the offset from the CTI base nanoseconds value.

### 5.1.5 CTI Signature
The CTI Signature is an optional feature that prevents a CTI message from a malicious source (which might have cloned an IP source address) from being accepted. A CTI message is sent in the clear followed by a CTI Signature. This permits implementations to use the contents of the CTI message without having to decrypt or decode each packet. For example, a system could be built in which the CTI message is received in real time but the CTI Signature is sampled on a random basis and not verified in real time. The full details of the CTI Signature are for a future version of this specification.

## 5.2 Operation

### 5.2.1 CTI Discovery & Configuration
For each CTI Session ID, several associations are required for proper CTI operation:  the TN shall have the association of CTI Session ID (pertaining to an O-RU interface) with the corresponding TU interface  the TN shall have the association of CTI Session ID with the corresponding CTI client (in O-DU) to which it has to communicate CTI-Beacon-Ack, CTI-Keep-Alive and possibly PON ranging notifications.  the O-DU shall have the association of CTI Session ID with the corresponding CTI server (in TN) to communicate

# 31 CTI reports and keepalives to.
Before the O-RU is installed, it is assumed that the OSS does not know which O-RU is associated with which transmission system (TU, TN). Further, since fronthaul takes a lot of bandwidth on the transmission system, it has to be a provisioned service. This section describes at least two ways that the two systems can learn of each other. In both of these procedures, the transport system comes up and is initialized. This then provides connectivity for the mobile system to come up and initialize. This implies that there is a least enough bandwidth on the transport system to provide M-plane support between the O-RU and O-DU. The next step is to then associate the mobile system with the transport system. The assumption is that the O-RU is an arbitrary unit that gets installed at an O-RU location.

# 3 Figure 5.7 : CTI Manual Discovery

# 4 Proposed procedure:
1. The installation technician interfaces with the OSS, either verbally or through a user interface, and enters identity information for the O-RU interface and TU interface 2. The TN OSS knows or is able to determine the association of the TU with the TN. The OSS system(s) initializes the O-DU and TN. The TN has the association of TU interface with O-RU interface (its CTI Session ID). The O-DU has the association of O-RU with TN (its CTI server) 3. CTI messaging can commence between the O-DU and TN The advantage of this approach is that it is very simple and, depending on how the cross provisioning is performed, does not necessarily require a coupling between the two OSS systems. The disadvantage is that the system is not automated.

# 14 5.2.1.2 Automatic Discovery using the OSS (Informative)
This section is superseded by section 6.2 of O-RAN CTI-TMP [4].

### 5.2.2 Operations
The CTI server and client shall operate as described in Figure 5.8. Figure 5.8 : CTI Configuration and Operational State Machines

# 3 The following operation is illustrated in Figure 5.8.
After necessary initial configuration, which is to be covered in the future Transport Management Plane Specification, a CTI interaction between a CTI client and a CTI server starts by including an exchange of CTI-Beacon message from the O-DU to the TN and its acknowledgement back from the TN to the O-DU. After reception of the CTI-Beacon-Ack message, both sides are operational for CTI. The CTI client and CTI server then interact according to the following: 1. The CTI client periodically sends a CTI-Report message to the CTI server with request information. This occurs no more than one CTI-Report per CTI Nominal message exchange time interval (CTI_NOM). If there is no internal request information, the CTI client shall not send a CTI-Report message to request bytes. The CTI client shall generate a CTI-Keep-Alive message at least once within the CTI Time Keep-Alive (CTI_KA).

# 13 2 The TN captures and processes CTI messages.
The CTI server shall generate a CTI-Keep-Alive message at least once within the CTI Time Keep-Alive (CTI_KA). 3. If the TN does not receive a CTI message (CTI-Report or CTI-Keep-Alive) within the CTI Time Out (CTI_TO), it shall suspend its CTI operation and return to the CTI configuration state. 4. If the O-DU does not receive a CTI-Keep-Alive message within the CTI Time Out (CTI_TO), it shall suspend its CTI operation and return to the CTI configuration state. The contents of the CTI-Report message are generated by the CTI client, which takes its inputs from the O-DU’s uplink scheduling decisions and from other operating entities within the O-DU. The CTI client gathers the uplink grant information from the RAN uplink scheduler over an interval described by the CTI Nominal message exchange time interval (CTI_NOM). This time is configured to be an integral number of mobile slot times. The choice of CTI_NOM shall follow the rules described in section 4.3.3.2. The CTI client should modify the local grant information from the O- DU RAN scheduler to make it represent future bytes to be transmitted over the Ethernet interface with sufficient margin for allowing for prediction uncertainties on the actual generated uplink fronthaul traffic.

## 5.3 Interface to OSS

### 5.3.1 Timers

# 6 Table 5.8 : CTI Timers
Name OSS OSS Min Max Description to TN to O-DU CTI Nominal x x 0,25 5 ms This value, abbreviated as CTI_NOM, is the minimum average interval message ms that a CTI-Report message is sent from the CTI client to the CTI exchange time server. CTI-Report messages may be sent less often. Because of interval queuing in the system, this value has to be interpreted as a rate and not as a spacing between packets. Typical values could be 1–2 ms for LTE, or lower for 5G. CTI Time Keep- x x 3 s This value, abbreviated as CTI_KA, is the maximum time interval Alive between consecutive CTI-Keep-Alive messages between the CTI client and the CTI server. CTI Time Out x x 10 s This value, abbreviated as CTI_TO, is the timeout value that a CTI Keep-Alive message needs to be received by the CTI client (O-DU) or the CTI server (transport system) before that respective system suspends CTI operations and returns to its CTI configuration state. CTI_TO shall be greater than CTI_KA, for example CTI_TO = N * CTI_KA with N being an integer greater than 1, to allow for the loss of one or several keepalives.

## 5.4 Examples of the CTI Pattern Descriptor for Fronthaul
A high-speed transport system such as a 10 Gbps PON system can have the ability to schedule bandwidth with the granularity of an 5G OFDMA symbol time which is on the order of 4.5μs to 71μs. However, sending CTI messages at this rate would result in too high a message rate. Further, describing bytes for every single symbol would result in excessively long CTI messages. In order to balance message frequency and length, a compression scheme based on 5G

# 19 TDD/FDD patterns is allowed.
The CTI pattern object model allows one entry in a CTI message to describe multiple transmissions over the network interface that follow a specific pattern. The intended use is to describe the bytes per symbol for each symbol or group of symbols within a mobile slot. The pattern of bytes per symbol within a mobile slot depends upon the 5G use of TDD or

# 23 FDD.
The total byte count for a pattern is always contained in the CTI table entry. If a non-zero pattern ID is used in the CTI reporting, there are two ways to interpret the CTI pattern parameters at the CTI server: Option 1) The CTI client is configured so that the total byte count is equal to the sum of the bytes per event within the pattern. This implies that for each different load in a mobile slot (different total byte count), a different pattern ID is needed. This can be used when the reporting may be coarse and not too many pattern IDs are needed. It is also possible to use a mix of explicit byte values for some symbols and a residual byte count (indicated by a reserved special value) for the other symbols. The absolute bytes for the residual symbols are deduced based on the CTI total byte count and the per-event explicit byte counts (see example 3 below). Option 2) If option 1 has a scalability issue, the alternative is to normalize the amount of bytes in each symbol so that the sum of all symbols is always the same value independently of the total reported byte count. The CTI server can then deduce the actual amount of bytes per symbol by using a multiplier (the reported total byte count divided by the normalized sum). This allows to re-use the same pattern ID for the same relative distribution of bytes across the symbols, by adding an extra calculation step at the CTI server. The choice between option 1) and option 2) is reflected by a dedicated configuration parameter per CTI session ID, so that the CTI client knows how to generate the values and the CTI server knows how to interpret the values.

Example 1: FDD pattern of 1 ms slot (n), 14 symbols, 1,000 bytes per symbol and same pattern but with 2,000 bytes per symbol in another 1 ms slot (m)

## 5.5 Other O-DU Functional requirements

### 5.5.1 Reporting scope
The O-DU shall be able to generate uplink bandwidth reports per O-RU, aggregated over all corresponding RAN schedulers for that O-RU. The O-DU shall be able to generate uplink bandwidth reports per O-RU interface, aggregated over all corresponding RAN schedulers for that O-RU interface. The CTI protocol additionally allows to generate uplink bandwidth reports per fronthaul Flow (Layer 2 / Layer 3 mapping).

### 5.5.2 Reporting accuracy
The reported bandwidth shall be at least equal to the actual upstream U-plane traffic generated by the O-RU (no underestimation). The accuracy of reported time references (Base + Offset) shall be better than 10µs (-5µs/+5µs).

### 5.5.3 O-DU CTI performance
The O-DU shall be characterized according to a CTI message rate category based on its supported CTI_MIN (as defined in section 4.3.3). When an equipment supports a category, all lower numbered categories shall also be supported. The O-DU shall be characterized according to a value of CTI message timing performance (as defined in section 6.2). These parameters shall be exposed to the OSS for configuration and management.

# 6 Time alignment between O-DU and Transport

## 6.1 Timing architecture options
The Fronthaul O-DU is scheduling in the future. The TN has to follow this by granting allocations aligned in time. This requires the timing of both systems to be time synchronized to a common reference for the grants to line up. There are three options to achieve this;  Using GNSS: Both the O-DU and the TN are independently synchronized using a GNSS source. There is no synchronization interaction needed between the O-DU and the TN.  Using IEEE PTPv2 (1588-2008): Both the O-DU and the TN have access to a common GM clock by using PTPv2. The PTP packets are either independently received by O-DU and TN, or the PTP packets are distributed to the TNs via O-DUs (e.g. when the GM resides in the O-DU).  Mix of both: The O-DU uses either GNSS or PTP, while the TN independently uses the other method. Note that the synchronization of the O-RU itself is not influenced by CTI and is out of scope of the CTI specification (see

# 15 O-RAN CUS [2] instead).

## 6.2 Resource allocation alignment
With CTI, the TN scheduler aligns its granting decisions on reporting by RAN schedulers, in order to follow traffic variations (per slot or per group of slots) of O-RUs. The better the time alignment precision of the TN scheduler to the uplink fronthaul traffic from the O-RUs, the lower the need for buffering uplink packets and hence the lower the upstream latency. The precision of aligment depends on two factors, as shown in Figure 6.1; Firstly, the arrival time of the CTI reporting message at the TN. The TN will need some processing time once the message is received before it can apply the updates of bandwidth scheduling to its TUs. This can be expressed as a minimal spacing (called “TN CTI message timing performance”) needed between the arrival time of the CTI message and the start boundary at Ra of the mobile slot N being reported in the message. A given TN equipment is characterized by a value of

# 26 CTI message timing performance.
The arrival time depends on the O-DU generation time, which depends on the necessary processing time after the RAN scheduler decisions were made for the corresponding slot. This can be expressed as the “O-DU CTI message timing performance”, the minimal spacing guaranteed by the O-DU between the generation time of the CTI message and the start boundary at Ra of the mobile slot N being reported in the message. The O-DU shall be characterized by a value of

# 31 CTI message timing performance.
The arrival time also depends on the transmission latency of the CTI message itself (in case of intermediate nodes between

# 33 O-DU and TN).
Figure 6.1 : Timing of CTI message generation by O-DU and reception at TN, limits for TN being able to apply bandwidth updates for the reported mobile slot. If the O-DU CTI message timing performance after subtraction with the maximal CTI transport latency still respects the TN CTI message timing performance, the TN can update the bandwidth for the mobile slot N on time. Note that as long as this condition is met, the jitter on arrival time of the CTI message will have no effect on the bandwidth updates and on the resulting fronthaul uplink latency. If the CTI messages arrive early, they have to be buffered in the TN until they need to be processed for their associated mobile slot (N). The earliest arrival time is just after the O-DU has made scheduling decisions for mobile slot (N), which is in the order of several mobile slot durations before the start of mobile slot (N). If the CTI messages arrive too late at the TN, the TN will only be able to apply the update for slot N in the next (or one of the next) bandwidth update opportunities by the TN, leading to buffering of the traffic of slot N at the TU, and hence an increase of latency. That latency depends on the granularity of TN to apply bandwidth updates per TU, and the previous bandwidth setting of the TN and buffer status of the TU. Secondly, assuming the CTI reporting message does arrive on time at TN, perfect alignment will not be possible due to sources of uncertainty that cannot be influenced or compensated by the O-DU:  Time granularity of TN to send bandwidth allocations.  Variation on Ta3_max per O-RU (based on its category), typically 20µs (see table B-5 in O-RAN CUS [2])  Possible mix of different O-RU categories on the shared distribution networks of the same TN. Note that the difference in propagation distance between different TUs is compensated by time equalization of the TUs by the TN. The actual latency (buffering + propagation) of each TU is brought to the same level, with the furthest TU having the longest propagation and shortest buffering, and the shortest TU having the shortest propagation and the longest buffering. In other words, the time equalization does not introduce an extra delay penalty, but it brings the propagation delay of all TUs to the level of the furthest TU. Figure 6.2 : Time alignment of O-DU scheduler decisions, CTI message generation, CTI message reception, TN scheduler updates, uplink traffic at O-RU R3 reference point. Example for two TUs at different distance from the TN.

# 7 Conclusion

## 7.1 Summary
This document specifies the TC-plane of CTI. TC-plane messages between O-DU and TN allow for the initialisation and operation of a CTI session, and for the exchange of future load requirements so that the TN scheduler can schedule the transport resource pro-actively, reducing the upstream latency of the fronthaul packets compared to a reactive TN scheduling system. The document includes (Chapter 4) a description of the context (topologies of interconnecting O-RUs to O-DUs via TNs aggregating multiple TUs on shared distribution networks), (Chapter 5) the required functions on the O-DU for supporting CTI exchange with TNs, the role of the parameters needed for CTI, the message types and formats, the protocol operation, the list of parameters, ways for associating the O-RU interface with corresponding TN managed entity, and (Chapter 6) the time alignment aspects between O-DU scheduler and TN scheduler.

## 7.2 Relationships and unicities in the context of encapsulation of CTI flows between CTI servers and CTI
Foreword This Technical Specification (TS) has been produced by O-RAN Alliance. Modal verbs terminology In the present document "shall", "shall not", "should", "should not", "may", "need not", "will", "will not", "can" and "cannot" are to be interpreted as described in clause 3.2 of the O-RAN Drafting Rules (Verbal forms for the expression of provisions). # 6 Release xx.yy.zz
where: xx the first digit-group is incremented for all changes of substance, i.e. technical enhancements, corrections, updates, etc. (the initial approved document will have xx=01). yy the second digit-group is incremented when editorial only changes have been incorporated in the document. zz the third digit-group included only in working versions of the document indicating incremental changes during the editing process. The present document describes the Transport Management Procedures for the Cooperative Transport Interface (CTI). CTI is an interface between O-DUs and Transport Nodes of a packet-based transport network that is used to interconnect the O-DUs to a variety of O-RUs. CTI specifically targets transport Nodes that manage a shared point-to- multipoint access network. Intermediate transport nodes (routers and switches) that only manage point-to-point links do not exchange CTI messages with the O-DUs. CTI consists of a Transport Control plane (TC) and a Transport Management (TM). This document specifies the TM Information Model / Data Model and procedures. The TC-plane is described in [1]. The reader is referred to the TC-plane document for a description of the protocol as well as background, context, motivation and topologies with CTI. This document focuses on the management aspect of CTI. The goals are to define the CTI-related configurable parameters at TN and at O-DU, to define a suitable set of YANG modules to capture these parameters, to describe necessary steps in the configuration of the parameters, and to define an auto-discovery method to automate the correlation between TN specific parameters and CTI parameters.

# 4 High Level Description

## 4.1 General CTI Management Architecture

### 4.1.1 Foreword on management domains
This document refers to separate “transport domain OSS” and “RAN domain SMO”, without any implication of ownership of the domains or use of particular processes or protocols in the transport domain OSS. Each domain is responsible for managing its nodes and can do so independently, but for CTI some level of mutual coordination is needed. Note that using two domains in this document does not preclude alternative approaches such as an integrated OSS for both domains, or an overarching orchestrating function that would select the parameters and forward them to the OSS domains.

### 4.1.2 Summary of architecture
As the configuration of CTI parameters in the O-DU is non real-time, it shall be done over the O-RAN O1 interface using NETCONF/YANG. This document does not make assumptions about the management process in the Transport OSS. Several CTI parameters are common for O-DU and TN side and have to be aligned. There is a need for coordination between both operation domains. This document specifies the needs, but does not make assumptions about the process or protocols to ensure such coordination. The only process described in this document is an automated auto-discovery which allows to link a TN specific transport parameter with each individual CTI session ID. This document does not make assumptions about the integration of functional features into physical nodes. For example, the document does not restrict the realization of the RAN domain DHCP server, which can be integrated with the O-DU, can be provided by the transport system, or can be accessed via a relay.

# 23 Figure 4.1 : Management architecture for CTI

### 4.1.3 Parameters to be configured
There are two types of parameters related to CTI:  Parameters to establish L2 or L2 + L3/L4 connectivity for CTI messages between CTI servers and CTI clients, to be configured by Transport OSS and by RAN SMO, and their corresponding YANG models  Parameters for the operation of CTI, to be configured by Transport OSS and by RAN SMO, and their corresponding YANG models

# 5 CTI Management

## 5.1 CTI connectivity parameters and configuration
This chapter describes how to enable CTI connectivity between the CTI servers and CTI clients. It is a conceptual description of the configuration needs and does not specify protocols or methods or sequences of actions for the configuration.

### 5.1.1 Point-point or switched Ethernet connectivity between TN and O-DU

# 7 5.1.1.1 L2 Connectivity parameters
The packets shall follow the Ethernet encapsulation as described in O-RAN CTI TCP [1]. The CTI packets are encapsulated in Ethernet with the invariant value of O-RAN Ethertype (0x9433), so the Ethertype is not configurable. The Ethernet Protocol Subtype (see O-RAN CTI TCP [1])) for O-RAN CTI is also an invariant value but not formally specified yet, so it is made configurable (value 0x1 is proposed in [1]). Note: This version of the document only specifies the use of single (.1Q) VLAN tag for CTI transport and L2 filter parameter. The use of dual VLAN-tag is to be specified in a later version of this document. Both O-DU and TN need to know the corresponding VLAN(s) and MAC addresses of respectively the CTI servers and CTI clients they have to connect to. As mentioned in O-RAN CTI TCP [1], each TN may host multiple CTI servers, each O-DU may host multiple CTI clients, and connectivity between all clients and servers shall be supported. The operator is free to choose how to segment the network with different VLANs, from a single flat model (option A: same VLAN configuration for CTI in the whole network) to differentiation (a VLAN configuration per TN-O-DU pair

# 20 (Option B) or per client-server pair (Option C)).

# 22 Figure 5.1 : Layer 2 interconnection options
Note (not shown in the figure) that an intermediate switch could perform VLAN translation between Transport domain and RAN domain. Note that the YANG model caters for all possibilities by defining a set of connectivity parameters per pair of CTI server

# 26 – CTI client.

# 27 5.1.1.2 Configuration of L2 connectivity parameters
Figure 5.2 : Configuration of Layer 2 connectivity parameters in case of Ethernet switching

# 4 The process involves following steps:
1) [per CTI server] CTI server MAC addr is stored in Transport OSS [per CTI client] CTI client MAC addr is stored in RAN SMO 2) [per CTI server and per CTI client] Transport OSS and RAN SMO exchange CTI server and CTI client MAC addresses from 1), and exchange [per (CTI client;CTI server) combination] the VLAN ID to be used 3) [per CTI client] Transport OSS configures MAC addr of CTI clients and VLAN IDs in TN [per CTI server] RAN SMO configures MAC addr of CTI servers and VLAN IDs in O-DU

### 5.1.2 IP routing connectivity between TN and O-DU

# 14 5.1.2.1 L2 + L3/L4 Connectivity parameters
The packets shall follow the UDP/IP/Ethernet encapsulation as described in O-RAN CTI TCP [1]. The CTI UDP listening port is invariant but not (yet) defined as a well-known port, so it is also still made configurable. Both O-DU and TN need to know the corresponding L2 and L3/L4 parameters to use for communicating with respectively the CTI servers and CTI clients they have to connect to. As mentioned in O-RAN CTI TCP [1], each TN may host multiple CTI servers, each O-DU may host multiple CTI clients, and connectivity between all clients and servers shall be supported. At Ethernet level, each CTI client and CTI server may have its own MAC address, and VLANs are used based on the subnetting at IP level. At IP level, subnetting defines how many IP addresses are used and how the different nodes will be interconnected;
- If all CTI servers and clients in the whole network are part of a single subnet (Option A), each client may use
single IP address (for communicating with all servers), each server may use a single IP addres (for communicating with all clients), and the TNs and O-DUs are connected by point-point links or intermediate switches.
- Alternatively, the network could be split in multiple subnets on a node level, where communication between
subnets happen via an intermediate router. Option B shows an example of one subnet at O-DU side and one subnet at TN side, interconnected by an intermediate router.
- Alternatively, the network could be split in multiple subnets along TN-O-DU combinations. Option C shows
an example of one subnet per O-DU, shared with all TNs. The CTI servers in the TNs support multiple IP addresses (one per subnet) and there is no need for routing between the TNs and O-DUs (e.g. intermediate switch).
- (note that sharing subnets across transport and RAN domains (options A and C) probably only apply to cases
of a single operator managing both domains). At UDP level, a single UDP listening port value is used for all clients, servers and messages. The source port value may be freely chosen. Its value remains the same during a communication session between the CTI client and CTI server, but may be ephemeral from one communication session to the next. Note that the YANG model caters for all possibilities by defining a set of connectivity parameters per pair of CTI server

# 8 – CTI client.

# 13 Figure 5.3 : Layer 3 interconnection options

# 14 5.1.2.2 Configuration of L2 connectivity parameters
Figure 5.4 a, b: Configuration of Layer 2 connectivity parameters in case of IP routing

# 4 The process involves following steps:
1) If subnets are shared between Transport and RAN domains (options A and C in section 5.1.2.1 and Fig 3-2a), the common VLAN IDs shall be coordinated between the Transport OSS and RAN SMO. Otherwise (Option B in section 5.1.2.1 and Fig 3-2b) this step is not needed. 2) [per CTI client] Transport OSS configures VLAN ID to be used for TC-plane [per CTI server] RAN SMO configures VLAN ID to be used for TC-plane The MAC addresses of the next hop is fetched by normal means (ARP) after configuration of L3 parameters (see section 5.1.2.3).

# 13 5.1.2.4 Remarks about layer 3 connectivity
The O-RU and the O-DU need routing table configuration (multiple subnets), this document doesn’t describe this configuration. Additionally, the DHCP relay agent in the first router facing the O-RU has to be be configured with the IP address of the DHCP server in the RAN domain to allow DHCP communication between the DHCP client in the O-RU and the

# 18 RAN DHCP server.
In some subnet cases there could be a router between the TN and O-DU. The configuration of the router is not described in this document. There could also be a NAT (NAPT) between the TN and O-DU. In that case there are a couple of attention points that need to be considered, namely the impact of destination port translation, the need of NAT traversal, etc… This is out of scope of this document.

# 6 CTI procedures
Proper interpretation of CTI messages by the TNs requires a level of cooperation between the CTI server side and CTI client side to guarantee consistency of the parameter values and and correlation between the parameters. Although it is possible to rely on manual correlation actions, it is beneficial to automate the process. This section describes an automated autodiscovery method of the correlation of the CTI session IDs with the TU/TN transport parameter they correspond to. The same method can also be used to determine which CTI server has to be associated per given CTI session ID.

## 6.1 Correlations to be performed
For proper operation of CTI, several parameters need to be consistent at both TN and at O-DU sides. This means that the same values have to be consistently configured at both CTI server and CTI client side by their respective management systems. The method or protocols for this coordination between Transport OSS and RAN SMO are out of scope of this document. Static parameters such as timer values, CTI Flow ID filters, CTI Pattern IDs etc… can be coordinated at OSS level independently of the topology of the O-RUs and transport nodes. Dynamically allocated parameters such as IP addresses of CTI servers and CTI clients are dependent of the interconnection topology of TNs and O-DUs, but not of the topology of the O-RUs. They can be coordinated at OSS level. The topology of O-RU deployments requires the following correlations for every CTI session ID, based which TU interface each O-RU interface is connected to (see Figure 6.1 for a logical view of the correlations. This figure is conceptual only and does not represent how or where the correlation have to be executed (in the TN or in its management system)):  The TN needs to determine which transport parameter has to be linked to the corresponding CTI session ID (combined with a CTI flow ID if used) in the CTI report messages (note that multiple transport parameters could be configured on a TU interface, only one pertains to a combination CTI session ID + CTI flow ID). CTI flow IDs are only unique per CTI client (different clients could use the same Flow ID for different meanings), so the CTI client shall be taken into account in the correlation.  The TN needs also to keep track of which CTI client is reporting the CTI session ID, to send messages related to that CTI session ID. A single CTI client may report about multiple CTI session IDs.  At O-DU side, the CTI client needs to correlate which CTI session ID to use for each O-RU interface it reports about. This is a one-to-one relationship. For reporting between different flows on the same CTI session ID the O-DU also needs to be aware of the class of service associated to each flow, which in turn is represented by a given set of L2/L3/L4 filter parameters reflecting how uplink traffic is tagged by the O-RU. This tagging could be different in different transport networks (a single O-DU can in principle manage O-RUs in multiple transport networks), so the CTI server (reflecting the TN) shall be taken into account in the correlation.  The O-DU also needs to know to which CTI server to send the reports for a given CTI session ID. Multiple reports could have to be sent to the same CTI server. It is recommended to use the physical MAC address of the O-RU port over which the O-RU has M-plane connectivity as the value of the CTI session ID. Figure 6.1 : O-RU topology-dependent correlations for CTI session IDs (conceptual only, for YANG elements please see Chapter 6)

## 6.2 Auto Discovery for correlation of CTI session ID to transport
parameter in TN This optional method is a means to automate the correlation of CTI session ID with the required transport parameter on the corresponding TU (or TU UNI) on the corresponding TU or TU UNI. It avoids relying on manual correlation during the installation phase of the O-RU to a given TU interface. The method is based on re-using the DHCP exchange from the O-RU that is performed during start up of the O-RU to achieve IP connectivity for the M-plane defined in O-RAN MP [4]. Both cases of layer 2 and layer 3 connectivity are very similar, using the DHCP relay agent in the TN to add the agent circuit ID as the key for the correlation. The only differences are the use of giaddr by the DHCP relay agent in case of layer 3 connectivity, and the mandatory use of IP in the C-plane and U-plane traffic in case of layer 3 connectivity. If the M-plane uses IPv4, the DHCP relay agent adds Option 82 as per IETF RFC 3046 [11], which contains the agent circuit ID (sub option code 1), which is a string uniquely identifying the TU interface on which the DHCP request was received. If the M-plane uses IPv6, the DHCPv6 relay agent adds Option 18 as per IETF RFC 3315 [12], which contains the agent circuit ID. Additionally, the possible use of DHCP Option 60 as per IETF RFC 2132 [13] and DHCP Option 124 as per IETF RFC3925 [14] by the O-RU is specified in O-RAN MP [4]. Even if such options are not used, the O-RU interface will be discovered by the RAN SMO during the autoconfiguration of the O-RU through M-plane exchanges. Once the O-RU is configured, the RAN SMO can correlate the agent circuit ID with the O-RU interface ID based on the allocated IP address. In turn the O-RU interface is uniquely linked to a CTI session ID. The correlation [agent circuit ID, CTI session ID] can then be notified back to the transport OSS, which pushes the correlation to the corresponding

# 25 TN that terminates the given TU.
It is recommended to use the unique MAC address of the O-RU interface as the CTI session ID. For IPv4 this is communicated to the DHCP server in the field “chaddr” of DHCP option 82. For IPv6 it can be communicated as “client link layer address” in DHCPv6 Option 79 as per IETF RFC 6939 [15]. If the O-RU does not use Option 79 in DHCPv6, there needs to be a preconfigured association [O-RU ID; MAC address] in the RAN SMO. The auto discovery method applies to cases where the O-RU shares the same physical interface for the M-plane and for the CUS-plane. The method does not apply to O-RUs using different interfaces for the CUS-plane. The following sections 6.2.1 and 6.2.2 supersede section 3.2.1.2 in O-RAN CTI TCP [1].

### 6.2.1 Switched Ethernet connectivity between O-RU and O-DU
Figure 6.2 : Auto-discovery method with Layer 2 interconnectivity The sequence of steps is as follows (example for IPv4); 1) O-RU starts by issuing DHCP discovery for its M-plane communication. The DHCP relay agent in TN adds option 82 to DHCP Discovery. Note that at start up the O-RU can be unaware of the configured M-plane VLAN ID. It can scan multiple VLAN IDs (and untagged) until receiving an answer from the O-DU side. Only DHCP messages with VLAN ID matching the configured M-plane VLAN ID will be passed through (with option 82 stamped) by the TN, all other messages are discarded by the TN. 2) O-RU gets M-plane IP configuration (by DHCP), starts up and gets configured by M-plane:
- Either options 60 or 124 are used that can fully identify O-RU ID
- Or the O-RU ID is discovered during O-RU configuration by the RAN SMO via the M-plane
3) Two associations are extracted and stored in the RAN SMO:
- RAN DHCP server extracts the association [assigned M-plane IP address; Agent Circuit ID; chaddr]
- If O-RU ID is present in DHCP options 60 or 124, the RAN domain DHCP server extracts the
association [assigned M-plane IP address; O-RU ID]. If the DHCP options 60 or 124 are not used, the association is extracted by RAN SMO.
- If DHCP server is hosted in the O-DU, the information is communicated to the RAN SMO over the

# 22 O1 interface
4) RAN SMO correlates [Agent Circuit ID; chaddr] with [O-RU ID] based on M-plane IP address. 5) RAN SMO configures O-DU (via O1) so that CTI client uses CTI session ID = chaddr for this O-RU ID. 6) RAN SMO informs Transport OSS with association [Agent Circuit ID; CTI session ID] 7) Transport OSS is able to determine the corresponding TN from “Access-Node-Identifier” in Agent Circuit ID, and then configures association (Circuit ID; CTI session ID) to that TN.

### 6.2.2 IP routing connectivity between O-RU and O-DU
Figure 6.3 : Auto-discovery method with Layer 3 interconnectivity The sequence of steps is as follows (example for IPv4); 1) O-RU starts by issuing DHCP discovery for its M-plane communication. The DHCP relay agent in TN adds option 82 to DHCP Discovery, adds “giaddr”, converts the message from broadcast to unicast, and forwards it to RAN DHCP server. Note that this requires that the DHCP relay agent in the TN is pre-configured with the IP address of the RAN DHCP server, as mentioned in section 5.1.2.4. Note that at start up the O-RU can be unaware of the configured M-plane VLAN ID (if it is used between TU and TN). The O-RU can scan multiple VLAN IDs (and untagged) until receiving an answer from the O-DU side. The TN will only process DHCP messages with a VLAN ID matching the configured M-plane VLAN ID, all others are discarded by the TN. The remaining steps 2 – 7 are identical to the steps in section 6.2.1. Note that the same approach can be taken in case the transport domain would be responsible to the IP configuration of the O-RUs (DHCP server hosted in the transport domain). This scenario is not worked out in this document as it is considered to be unlikely.

## 6.3 Auto discovery for correlation of CTI session ID to CTI server
There needs to be a pre-configuration at Transport OSS of Agent cicuit ID (only the relevant fields) to Server (Server Name and MAC address in case of L2 connectivity for CTI). This association needs to be communicated to the RAN

# 21 SMO.
After the auto discovery of 6.2, the RAN SMO knows the Agent circuit ID per O-RU (interface), and the CTI session ID per O-RU (interface). It can then associate the CTI session ID of that O-RU (interface) to its corresponding CTI server based on the TN-identifying portion of the Agent circuit ID.

## 6.4 Performing correlations without Auto Discovery method
In this case the correlations are not facilitated by an automated exchange of messages, and involve a manual configuration during installation of each O-RU, and several extra coordination steps between Transport OSS and RAN

# 29 SMO;
1) the correlation of CTI session ID to O-RU (interface) needs to be done at installation time, by manually populating the association of an O-RU (interface) identifier to a TU (interface) indentifier in the Transport OSS. It is then up to the Transport OSS to correlate the O-RU (interface) further to the transport parameter based on the TU (interface) identifier, and if needed to ask for the associated CTI session ID to the RAN SMO (in case the O-RU identifier that is visible to the Transport operator would be another identifier than the CTI session

# 35 ID).
2) the correlation of CTI session ID to a given CTI server needs an extra level of coordination between the Transport OSS and the RAN SMO. Based on the manual association in step 1), the Transport OSS can deduce the corresponding CTI server for a given CTI session ID based on the TU identifier (which is linked to a given TN user-facing port, which in turn is controlled by a given CTI server). The Transport OSS then communicates the association of CTI session ID (or the O-RU identifier) with the associated CTI Server name (and MAC address in case of L2 connecivity for CTI) to the RAN SMO.

# 7 CTI Information Model

## 7.1 General structure of the Information Model
The model in this document applies to the O-DU. Part of this model is common for the TN, but the specification of the IM of the TN is out of scope of this document. TN considerations (IM and DM) in this document are provided as informational examples. This version of the document provides the CTI IM itself and a partial integration of the CTI IM into the broader O-DU IM (see Figure 7.6). The full integration into the broader O-DU IM (choice of IOC as attachment point for CTIConfig IOC) is subject to further study and optimization in a future version of the document. The logical structure of the CTI IM at O-DU is determined by following facts;  When an O-DU supports the optional CTI functionality, it may have one or multiple CTI clients. Each O-DU has a separate “CTI Function” IOC, that contains one or multiple CTI clients. Each CTI client has a separate

# 13 IOC “CTIClient” that shall be configured.
 For each O-DU, the possible CTI server(s) that its CTI client(s) connect to shall be represented by a MOI

# 15 “CTIServer”.
 In one O-DU, each CTI client may have connectivity to multiple remote CTI servers, and each such CTI server may have connectivity to multiple CTI clients in the O-DU (in other words a full mesh of CTI servers and CTI clients is supported).  Each pair of CTI server and CTI client shall use a “CTIConnProfile” for the exchange of CTI messages between the pair. A CTIConnProfile may be used by multiple server-client pairs.  CTISessions of a given CTI client are grouped per corresponding CTI Server into a “CTISessionGroup”.  CTIFlow(s) are configured per CTI server and e be referred by “CTIFlowsInUse” in one or multiple CTI sessions (of one or multiple CTI clients).  “CTISession” for each CTIClient and “CTIFlowsInUse” for each CTISession shall also be configured before the CTI functionality starts to work.  There are network-wide definitions of CTI patterns. The same pattern has the same meaning for all CTI servers and CTI clients. Depending on its position in the YANG structure, a parameter may be unique for the whole node, or only within a smaller context in the node allowing for multiple values to be configured inside the same node. Additionally, if a parameter needs to be unique across the whole network, this consistency shall be assured by the SMO system to configure the same value in all its managed nodes.

# 34 CTI Session ID:
The CTI Session ID shall be unique across the whole network. Recommendation is to use the MAC address of the O-

# 36 RU interface it is linked to.
The CTI session ID element is used as the cornerstone in the TN and O-DU YANG models.

# 39 CTI Session Group:
In each CTI Client the CTI sessions are regrouped per associated CTI Server.

# 42 O-RU ID or O-RU interface ID:
They are used locally in the O-DU, so in principle only unique within one O-DU. But it is more practical if it is unique across the whole network.

# 45 They are not used in the TN.

# 11 Pattern characteristics linked to a CTI Pattern ID:
From O-DU point of view a Pattern ID shall represent the same pattern characteristics no matter on which TN an O-RU is connected to. The Pattern ID may therefore be unique at O-DU node level. It is up to the RAN SMO to configure consistent values across the different O-DUs. From TN point of view a same Pattern ID could be re-used by accident by two different RAN networks (sets of O-DUs) while representing different pattern characteristics. The CTI Pattern ID is therefore defined at a per-CTI client level in the TN, allowing to make such differentiation.

# 19 L2, L3, L4 Parameters for CTI connectivity:
As mentioned in section 5.1, different sorts of connectivity may be used between pairs of clients and servers. The use of L2, L3 and L4 parameters are part of the network-wide planning. In the O-DU the parameters are kept in the CTI Client, CTI Server, and CTI connectivity profile. The CTI client keeps its MAC address (in case of Ethernet connectivity). The CTI Server keeps its connectivity type, its MAC address (in case of Ethernet connectivity) or its host (in case of UDP/IP connectivity). The CTI connectivity profile may be used between one or multiple pairs of CTI Client and CTI Server and keeps its connectivity type, the VLAN tag in case of Ethernet connectivity or the VLAN tag in case of UDP/IP connectivity, and the client host (in case of UDP/IP connectivity). A similar approach could be taken in the TN to group connectivity parameters per pair of CTI server and CTI client, see

# 33 CTI timers
It is assumed that there is no difference in timer values throughout the network, their values shall be unique.

# 36 UDP listening port
When UDP/IP is used for CTI transport between a CTI client and a CTI server, all messages between all CTI servers and all CTI clients over all networks shall use the same destination port value. Without a well-known IANA port, a single value shall be consistently configured in all TN and O-DU nodes.

# 41 CTI versions
Each TN could support one or more versions, each O-DU may support one or more versions. The supported versions are a list structure in the O-DU and in the TN. Each CTI client shall know what versions are supported by a given CTI server, and vice versa. Hence the CTI version to be used is defined per CTI client in the TN, per CTI server in the O-

# 45 DU.
Please note there is no direct version negociation mechanism in CTI between a CTI client and a CTI server, it is up to the management to select the appropriate version to be used. Ethertype and Protocol subtype values when CTI directly encapsulated in L2 The values for the O-RAN Ethertype and CTI Protocol Subtype are invariant over all networks.

This DT groups attributes that describe the status of the exchange of CTI messages between a given CTI Client and a given CTI Server.

# 16 Rules for configuration:
Each CTIClientServerStatus instance describes one pair of CTI Client – CTI Server, hence refers to only one CTI Server. There shall be one instance for each Server that this Client communicates with.

# 19 Monitoring:
The ctiClientServerConnStatus reflects the status of the CTI keep-alive exchange between the client and a given server and is read-only. “True” signifies that the keepalives are received as expected from the given server. “False” signifies that keepalives from the given server have been not been received for longer than the time out duration (ctiTo).
