# 11 11.5.2.1 Forwarding Adjacency architecture for cross domain scale
Forwarding Adjacency abstracting the path between domain boundary routers is one of the ways to optimize and scale a controller based Xhaul architecture. Forwarding Adjacency architecture is based on following architectural concepts:
- Transport network is divided into multiple smaller routing domains. Routing domains can
be represented by separate BGP autonomous systems, or separate IGP domains (areas). Or, combination of BGP autonomous systems and IGP areas, where BGP autonomous systems are further divided with IGP areas.
- The size of each routing domain might vary, but must be chosen in such a way, that even
the weakest transport device in given routing domain can participate in intra-domain routing and intra-domain MPLS path (SR, SR-TE, Flex-Algo, RSVP, LDP) establishment without any scaling concerns
- Head-end router (border router) of intra-domain LSP advertises the intra-domain LSP (of
any kind, i.e. SR, SR-TE, Flex-Algo, RSVP, LDP) as standard link in BGP Link State (LS) topology database, with attributes similar to standard link, like for example SR Adjacency-SID, administrative group (link color, link affinity), SRLG, etc. IGP forwarding adjacency is established (RFC 4206) between domain border routers creating abstracted topology of the routing domain.
- BGP-LS (RFC 8571) is used to distribute abstracted topology. Given the fact that only
border routers, and only abstracted forwarding adjacency links between these border routers are exported, the size of the topology database exported via BGP-LS is considerably smaller. BGP-LS distribution can happen in two way, depending on the overall network scale o BGP-LS topology is exchanged between routers in different routing domains o BGP-LS topology is exchanged between PCEs in distributed PCE layer The first approach is more suitable for small to medium scale deployments. In this approach, any Transport Network Equipment has the detailed topology visibility of the local routing domain, and abstracted (with Forwarding Adjacencies advertised as links in BGP-LS) visibility of the remote routing domains. This significantly reduces the topology database stored on the Transport Network Equipments, therefore, in small/medium deployments PCE might not be necessary. The headend PE, based on the full topology database (detailed topology from local routing domain + topology abstracted with links representing forwarding adjacencies from remote routing domains), performs calculation of end-to-end SR-TE paths (local constrained shortest path first – CSPF – calculation). Each forwarding adjacency is represented in the resulting SR-TE label stack as single Adjacency-SID associated with given forwarding adjacency, regardless of the underlying ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 MPLS transport used for given forwarding adjacency. At each border node, this Adjacency SID is mapped to the actual transport label stack (LDP, RSVP, SR, SR-TE) used for the given forwarding adjacency.

# 5 This concept is outlined in Figure 11-10.

# 7 Figure 11-10 Forwarding Adjacency architecture
As further scaling optimization of this architecture, ingress PEs (typically cell site routers, with limited control plane resources required for efficient end-to-end path computation) can be off- loaded from end-to-end path computation. Distributed PCEs (Path Computation Elements) can be placed on more powerful transport devices (for example pre-aggregation or aggregation routers), or containerized/virtualized PCE function can be placed in the distributed telco cloud environment to execute end-to-end path computation duties over simplified (via forwarding adjacencies) full network topology. In this scenario, ingress PE requests from PCE on demand path computation for unresolved next-hops, as outlined in Figure 11-11. #### 11.5.2.2 Using Binding SID (BSID) for cross domain scale
As mentioned earlier, a controller-based architecture make use of the PCE to provides the SID list to the headend for an end-to-end path across multiple domains. If no constraints are imposed on the traffic, the SID list would consist of Area Border Routers Prefix SIDs as next hop. Traffic within the domain will use IGP to get to the next hop while utilizing well established IGP routing mechanism such as Equal Cost Multi Path (ECMP), metric based best path etc. At the ABR, the top most SID is popped and the new next hop SID/Label is exposed, starting the routing within the next IGP are or domain. The process is repeated until traffic reaches its destination. Figure 11-12 shows such behaviour between IGP Domain 0,1 and 2.

# 23 Figure 11-12 Basic SID list with no constraints
There may be scenarios where more explicit path considerations and constraints could be required, such as using low latency path or inclusion/exclusion of certain links or node. In those scenarios, rather than provide a SID list that encompasses every link/node through the path, mechanisms such as Flex Algo could be used to optimize the SID list on the head end. Figure 11-13 shows a scenario with latency and link/node constraints across the path. In this case operator may use Flex-Algo within a domain and use the PCE controller to provide SID list to the headend accordingly. Notice while the SID depth is no different from the earlier scenario Figure 11-13) and while it still only contain prefix-SIDs of ABR as next hop label, the SID’s now refer to the node’s Flex-Algo Prefix SID, instead of default algo SID. Due to this, the traffic behavior is also different and the next Hop

# 34 SID automatically uses the desired constraints-based path.
ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 3 Figure 11-13 Constraint based SID list with Flex-Algorithm
In scenarios where an operator is unable or unwilling to use Flex-Algo for SID list optimization, an SRTE Binding SID (BSID) could be used. A Binding SID is a fundamental component of Segment Routing network that may be used to provide SID and network scaling. A BSID is a SID that is associated with an SRTE policy’s active path and is a representation of an End-to-End candidate path. BSIDs could be used to provide additional scale by using nested SRTE policies across domains. The PCE instead of providing a full path through multiple domains, may provide the headend with a path within its own domain and a BSID corresponding to the next domain. When, exposed at the domain boundaries, the BSID gets translated into another set of SID List, providing extensibility and scalability throughout the topology. This process is shown in Figure 11-14.

# 18 Figure 11-14 SID scaling using binding SID
Figure 11-14 compares the two scenarios where an End-to-End path is required with latency and link/nodes constraints along the path. The first scenario is where the PCE provides a full SID list to the headend for the entire path, with based path is required end to end. The second scenario uses a Binding, exposed at domain boundaries and then use the appropriate constrains based SID within the domain in question. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 If an operator wishes to implement controller based architectural scaling, in addition to underlying segment-routing based transport with controllers, a device will need to support: [R35]: SHOULD support Binding SID as per draft-ietf-pce-binding-label-sid [175]

## 11.6 MPLS Quality of Service
The MPLS data plane includes a 3-bit field in the MPLS header, the TC – Traffic Class (previously EXP - Experimental) bits. These bits are assignable as a marker for QoS mechanisms in transport nodes to use as a classification and marking tool. The per-hop behavior for MPLS forwarding elements can be defined based on these markings. Because of the restricted size of the TC field, the specific markings are not standardized, but are open for individual operators to define. For a full discussion of a proposed marking scheme and QoS architecture for TNEs in Xhaul, see Chapter 14.

## 11.7 MPLS OAM
Basic OAM tools are Ping and Traceroute. Ping is required to test liveliness to a remote MPLS underlay destination and traceroute is required to trace paths and perform hop-by-hop fault isolation to remote MPLS underlay destination. The following capabilities are required on all TNEs. [R36]: MUST support “Detection of MPLS Data Plane Failures”, RFC8029 [127] [R37]: MUST support LSP Ping/Traceroute for SR IGP Prefix-SID and IGP Adjacency-SID with MPLS Data Plane, as defined in RFC8287 [133]

## 11.8 IP/MPLS service infrastructure
For IPv4, IPv6 and Ethernet services an overlay solution is used. Please refer to section 13 for a description of overlay service recommendations for a 5G Xhaul infrastructure.

# 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based
This document presents two packet switched underlay technologies, the first based on MPLS contained in section 11 and the second based on SRv6 contained in this section (section 12). An operator wishing to implement the transport architecture outlined in this document will need to select one of the two and implement the requirements outlined in the associated section. It should be noted that other transport architectures are potentially available but not covered in this revision of the document. This section outlines a packet switched underlay model based on SRv6. SRv6 is based on the segment routing architecture as defined in RFC8402 [139]. For more information on Segment Routing see annex A. In an SRv6 infrastructure, like an MPLS environment, it is important to consider the underlay / fabric of the transport infrastructure somewhat separately from the services that run on-top of the infrastructure. The emphasis with the underlay / fabric is to provide an environment that will scale and support the services required by a 5G infrastructure. In contrast, the services infrastructure runs on-top of the underlay/fabric of the transport network and supports the different components of the 5G infrastructure (Fronthaul,

# 40 Midhaul, Backhaul).
This chapter is specific to an SRv6 underlay/fabric, its data plane, control plane and how to scale it. Although there are some similarities with an SR-MPLS environment, in terms of architecture, there ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 are some key differences in requirements and particularly on how to scale the underlay infrastructure, which is critical in a 5G environment. The service infrastructure and how to support 5G service requirements for both SR-MPLS and SRv6 are covered in a common services section (section 13) as the technologies used and the designs have many similarities.

## 12.1 SRv6 data plane
SRv6 relies on an IPv6 data plane with segments defined using SIDs contained in the IPv6 header. SRv6 SIDs are specified in “Segment Routing Header” (SRH) and standardised in RFC8754 [151].

# 10 Packet switching TNEs supporting SRv6 will need to:
[R38]: MUST support “IPv6 Segment Routing Header (SRH)” RFC8754 [151] [R39]: MUST support “SRv6 Network Programming”, RFC8986 [154] [D30]: SHOULD support “Compressed SRv6 Segment List Encoding in SRH”, draft-ietf-spring- srv6-srh-compression [178]

## 12.2 SRv6 control plane
The SRv6 control plane refers to routing and path control within the SRv6 underlay/fabric. This infrastructure can extend to customer devices or stop at a Provider Edge (PE) function. Its role can be summarised as learning the topology, calculation, and implementation of dynamic and explicit routes across the SRv6 infrastructure and providing rapid protection and repair mechanisms. In a packet switched transport network consisting of a large number of routers, a mix of WAN and data centers components, the need to support traffic engineering, the underlay control plane is a typically a collection of independent routing domains that interact in a collaborate fashion.

# 28 Figure 12-1 SRv6 underlay architecture
Figure 12-1 illustrates how a large packet-switched transport infrastructure might be designed and how different components interact. It should be noted that not all these components are required, and some serve the same purpose but in different ways. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 1. Each routing domain has an IGP for internal connectivity. 2. Mechanisms to calculate SR policies or Traffic Engineer paths and convey them to the source nodes. Figure 12-1 shows a distributed “Path Computation Element” (PCE), with “Path Computation Element Protocol” (PCEP) running between the edge nodes and the PCE but there are other network-based mechanisms to calculate SR policies such as Flex-algo running in the IGP or head-end calculated paths. 3. Mechanisms to convey routing between IGP domains. This could be provided by summarization and redistribution, E-BGP between AS boundaries or via a multi-domain “Path Computation Element” (PCE). One of the key differences between an MPLS and IPv6 based underlay is that IPv6 enables address summarization within routing domains and also between routing domains. This makes an IPv6 based underlay network more scalable and less complex than a corresponding MPLS solution. 4. Mechanisms to convey topology and network state information from the network to the PCE and other central management elements. BGP Link State (BGP-LS) and Telemetry feeds are recommended tools to fulfil this requirement.

# 16 12.2.1 Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) for SRv6
SRv6 requires at least one IPv6 IGP per routing domain or autonomous system. There are two IGPs that support SRv6; ISIS for IPv6 or OSPFv3. They are both link-state protocols and have similar capabilities but there are operational differences which is beyond the scope of this document. The IGP provides internal connectivity within a routing domain. The size of a routing domain is determined by technical, operational and organizational considerations, such as protocol scalability and spans of control. In large networks, such as a 5G infrastructure, extending from the access to the transport core, it is very common to see multiple autonomous systems, IGPs and segmentation within the IGPs. In an SRv6 environment the IGP is responsible for distributing node, prefix and SID information to all nodes within the routing domain and for calculating the forward tables between these nodes. Optionally it can provide fast convergence mechanisms and distribute traffic engineering attributes within the domain and build multiple transport planes. Both IS-IS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 have facilities to create a hierarchical routing structure within a routing domain using levels and areas respectively. They also have the facility to bring external routing information into a routing domain and push routing information into other routing domains using route redistribution. Note: There are other techniques to achieve route re-distribution between routing domains, such as

# 36 BGP and centralised SDN controllers.
Note: When looking at SRv6 IGP requirements, there are sets of requirements for ISIS for IPv6 and OSPFv3. Operators need to follow the requirements associated with IGPs they are using within their network infrastructure.

# 40 12.2.1.1 Topology Independent Loop Free Alternative (TiLFA)
In the SRv6 underlay design outlined in this document TiLFA can be used to achieve fast IGP convergence in the event of a network failure. Topology Independent Loop Free Alternative as defined “Topology Independent Fast Reroute” using Segment Routing [174] is an IGP capability supported by Segment Routing that provides a local repair mechanism that achieves 100% coverage within a routing domain against links, nodes and SRLGs failures with convergence times, once failure detection has occurred, H/W dependent but typically less than 50ms. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 For each destination in the network, TI-LFA pre-installs a backup forwarding entry for each protected destination ready to be activated upon detection of the failure of a link used to reach the destination. TI-LFA provides protection in the event of any one of the following: single link failure, single node failure, or single SRLG failure. In link failure mode, the destination is protected assuming the failure of the link. In node protection mode, the destination is protected assuming that the neighbor connected to the primary link has failed. In SRLG protecting mode, the destination is protected assuming that a configured set of links sharing fate with the primary link has failed (e.g. a linecard or a set of links sharing a common transmission pipe). The mechanics of the TiLFA for SRv6 at failure is shown in Figure 12-2 and upon convergence in Figure 12-3. One of the key advantages of TiLFA over some other fast convergence mechanisms, not well illustrated in the example below, is that the TiLFA backup path is the same as the post convergence path, thus minimising micro-loops that can occur as IGPs converge.

# 17 Figure 12-2 TiLFA at failure with SRv6
ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 5 12.2.1.2 IGP Flexible-Algorithm
IGP Flexible-Algorithm is an IGP based traffic engineering technique that permits multiple forwarding tables to be created in the IGP based on operator programmed criteria. It is a simple, automatic way, in which a packet switched transport network can be traffic engineered, using only the IGP, to create different transport planes designed to meet specific operator defined criteria. Standard ISIS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 use the IGP metric on links and the “Shortest Path First” (SPF) algorithm to calculate the “best” path between an ingress and egress point in the network. For many services this approach is sufficient, however this approach cannot, for example, take into account real-time link latency, utilization, packet loss and whether an ECMP path shares links using the same underlying fibre ducts. IGP Flex-Algo, defined in RFC 9350 [160] is an IGP based Segment Routing traffic engineering capability, that enables an operator to define their own custom algorithm, based on a wide range of variables including: link latency, packet loss, bandwidth, affinity and shared risk link groups (SRLG), to achieve a specific forwarding aim. This is illustrated in Figure 12-4. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 12 12.2.2 SRv6 Traffic Engineering
SRv6 supports two forms of SR policies or SR Traffic Engineering. Both solutions rely on the IGP to gather and convey topological and resource information around the network and optionally to a Path Computation Element (PCE) optimized for SR via BGP-LS.

# 16 12.2.2.1 Segment Routing Traffic Engineering (SR-TE)
The SR policy consists of a list of SIDs the packet needs to traverse and is programmed into the packet on the source node. The SID list can consist of a mix of prefix and adjacency SIDs. In SR this form of TE allows a path to be: 1. Loosely source routed where some intermediate points, but not all, are specified between the ingress and egress node. Paths between these intermediate points typically use the shortest path, ECMP based routing determined by the IGP. 2. Explicitly source routed where all intermediate points and even links are specified between the ingress and egress nodes. In all cases, topology information and live network status within a routing domain is distributed within a routing domain by the IGP with suitable extensions. In single routing domain environments path computation can be performed either by individual head-end routers or via a centralised “SR Path Computational Element” (SR-PCE). In multi-domain routing environments, then path computation generally occurs on a “centralised SR-PCE” component that has topology information for all domains being traversed. This function can be a standalone entity or be integrated into strategically placed TNEs. This form of traffic engineering can support loose and explicitly routed paths, low-latency paths, bandwidth-guaranteed paths, and disjoint paths. Precise TE capability depends on the capabilities of the SR-PCE component.

# 36 12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm
IGP Flexible-Algorithm is described in section 12.2.1.2. It is an IGP based traffic engineering technique that permits multiple logical topologies to be created in an IGP domain based on operator programmed criteria. When used in a single IGP routing domain the IGP calculates and maintains the path. The ingress node simply needs to address the packet to the “locator-block” associated with the flexible algorithm. This removes the need for a head-end or centralised PCE path computation element and also keeps SID list to a minimum. This works in a single IGP domain but depending on area border router and autonomous system border router capabilities can be supported in multi-domain environments based on redistribution. For flex-algo requirements in an SRv6 environment see section 12.2.1.3 and 12.2.1.4. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 13 2. Inter-domain IGP redistribution

# 14 3. Inter AS BGP

# 15 4. Controller based

# 17 12.2.3.1 IGP based hierarchy
Both ISIS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 have the concept of routing hierarchy in their basic designs. In an SRv6 environment, route summarization or injection of a default route between IS-IS levels or OSPFv3 areas is sufficient to enable EVPN or L3VPNs services to be built over an SRv6 hierarchical IGP infrastructure.

# 23 12.2.3.2 Inter-domain IGP redistribution
One or more routers are located on the boundary between two or more IGP routing domains. These routers run multiple IGP instances, so have routing awareness of all the IGPs they participate in. Routing information is mutually re-distributed between the IGP protocols allowing reachability between the domains. This redistribution can be in the form of full routing, summarised routes or even default routes. The choice is dependent on the level of awareness required between domains. See Figure 12-5 for more detail. IGP route re-distribution in both IS-IS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 is a common capability.

# 33 12.2.3.3 Inter-AS BGP based routing
A router in each autonomous system exchanges routing information using BGP-4 supporting the IPv6 address family. It should be noted that this scheme provides better separation than inter- domain IGP redistribution but typically requires separate routers in each autonomous system.

# 37 See Figure 12-6 for more detail.

# 39 12.2.3.4 Controller based path calculation
In this scenario no routing information is exchanged between routing domains at the device level. Instead, each routing domain provides its topology to an SR Path Computation Element (SR-PCE), which is a central SDN control element responsible for determining and finding routes to a destination node on behalf of a source node. Although the SR-PCE is logically a central component, for scale and resiliency reasons it can consist of multiple individual entities distributed around and ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 serving different parts of the network. In this case the source TNE requires very limited visibility of the overall network, as end to end cross-domain path computation is delegated to the SR-PCE.

# A SR-PCE function in an SRv6 underlay transport network has three main functions.
1. Gather data about the topology of the overall SRv6 network underlay. Several options exist: a. The SR-PCE participates in the IGP domains and directly collects each domains IGP link-state database. b. Use BGP Link-State (BGP-LS) with appropriate extensions for SRv6 to collect the IGP’s link-state database from each routing domain. This is done through one or more BGP session between the SR-PCE and a TNE in each routing domain participating in the domain’s IGP. The TNEs retrieve information from the IGP LSDB and distribute it to the controller using the BGP link-state address family. 2. Communications between the PCE and PCC (path computation client) which is the headend TNE. In this document it is assumed to PCEP (path computation Element Protocol) is used as the communication mechanism between the source TNE and the SR-PCE. 3. Path computation. The PCE uses information gathered from the various domains to compute an SR policy consisting of a SID list which packets using the SR policy will traverse. This SID list can be a loosely sourced routed or explicitly source routed.

## 12.3 Scaling an SRv6 underlay infrastructure
Scaling is one of the key challenges in building a packet switched infrastructure supporting 5G services. Communications and support of L2 and L3 VPN services between two SRv6 TNEs relies entirely on IP routing mechanisms on the underlay transport fabric. In SRv6 this is based on longest IP prefix matching and forwarding, so TNEs can support routing and forwarding based on full IPv6 host routes, summarized IPv6 routes or default routing or a combination, derived from dynamic routing protocols or statically defined. Further, different TNEs in the end to end path can use different levels of route summarization appropriate to their position in the network and their computation, memory and NPU/ASIC resources.

# 29 12.3.1 Route summarization and redistribution
Summarization within ISIS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 is part of the base protocol capability and can occur between levels in IS-IS for IPv6 and between areas in OSPFv3 using “Area Border Routers” (ABRs). Summarization is also a common capability when redistributing routes between different routing domains and is also supported between Autonomous Systems using BGP-4 between “Autonomous System Border Routers” (ASBRs). This is illustrated in Figure 12-5 and Figure 12-6 and shows how PE1-4’s routing tables can be controlled through route summarization. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 3 Figure 12-5 Summarization / redistribution using IGPs

# 6 Figure 12-6 Summarization / redistribution using BGP-4
This approach offers considerable flexibility, as operators can choose the level of summarization, ranging from no summarization to default routing between domains depending on the size of the network and level of awareness required between domains. It can also offer inter-domain traffic engineering support based on flexible algorithm within an IGP domain. However, there are some considerations and limitations: 1. Address planning is critical and needs to occur upfront. 2. Route summarization might result in sub-optimal routing in certain designs. 3. Some traffic engineering scenarios cannot be achieved with route summarization alone. 4. A source TNE cannot rely on a host route withdrawal to detect a remote TNE failure covered by a summary route. In this situation over forms of device or service verification are required. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 [D33]: ABRs SHOULD have flex-algorithm aware summarization/redistribution function. This is a local behavior. To use BGP-4 to transmit underlay SRv6 routing between Autonomous Systems requires: [R48]: BGP with IPv6 multi-protocol extensions (RFC1771, RFC2545, RFC2858) [43][50][55]

# 8 12.3.2 Controller based scaling
Route summarization and redistribution is simple and allows massive scale and allows end to end traffic engineering based on flex-algo. However, some traffic engineering scenarios cannot be achieved, such as path diversity and bandwidth optimization, because summarization hides topological details. To achieve more complex TE solutions, end-to-end visibility of the network is required, and a controller-based solution based on an SR-PCE is used. The SR-PCE receives detailed topology information via BGP-LS protocol from each domain. The SR-PCE then has a full picture of end to from SR-PCE via PCEP protocol. SR-PCE responds with stack of SIDs to establish path to egress

# 18 12.3.3 SRv6 scaling conclusion
To build an underlay transport network that is highly scalable and supports traffic engineering the simplest way is to uses a multi-domain IGP that supports flex-algo and use address summarization. This design might not be sufficient for all application requirements. In these instances, a PCE based solution could be deployed in tandem for TE use cases that require additional network visibility.

## 12.4 IPv6 Quality of Service
The IPv6 packet includes a 6-bit field in the IPv6 header, the DiffServ Code Point (DSCP). These bits are assignable as a marker for QoS mechanisms in transport nodes to use as a classification and marking tool. The per-hop behavior for IPv6 forwarding elements can be defined based on these markings. For a full discussion of a proposed marking scheme and QoS architecture for TNEs in

# 28 Xhaul, section 14.

## 12.5 SRv6 OAM
SRv6 OAM functionality is required to understand the status of the network. SRv6 OAM is described in “Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) in Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)” RFC 9259 [159]

Ping is required to test liveliness to a remote SRv6 underlay address and traceroute is required to trace paths and perform hop-by-hop fault isolation to remote SRv6 underlay address. The following capabilities are required on all TNEs. [R53]: TNEs MUST support ICMPv6 (RFC4443) [83] [R54]: TNEs MUST support IPv6 ping to query liveliness of a remote IPv6 address along the shortest path for default SPF algorithm. ## 12.6 SRv6 Service infrastructure
An SRv6 transport underlay supports basic IPv6 services natively at the control and data plane. For Ethernet, IPv4 and IPv6 VPN services an overlay control plane infrastructure is used to convey VPN connectivity information. At the data plane the P devices can utilise a standard IPv6 data plane with the PE devices requiring an IPv6 data plane with SRv6 VPN network programming awareness [154]. # 13 Packet-switched Xhaul services Infrastructure
To support an Xhaul environment requires the packet switched network to support L2 and L3 services. Both an MPLS and IPv6 packet switched underlays use EVPN to support L2 and MP-BGP

# 4 L3VPNs.

## 13.1 MP-BGP design
Both EVPN and MP-BGP L3VPNs use MP-BGP, with appropriate address-family support for EVPN and L3VPN, to convey service connectivity information between Provider Edge (PE) equipment. Typically, the MP-BGP infrastructure for L2 and L3 services uses a Route Reflector design rather than an I-BGP mesh between all PEs. In large networks, operators will normally implement a hierarchical Route Reflector (RR) design for Multi-Protocol BGP (MP–BGP) peering. A pair of Route Reflectors (RR) could be used at every domain to provide scalability and extensibility. Figure 13-1 Hierarchical Route Reflector Design for Multiple Protocol BGP Figure 13-1 shows the Hierarchical Route Reflector Design utilizing RR pairs in each network domain, all peering with National Route Reflector core.

# 18 13.3.2 Constraints based Traffic Steering in L3VPNs
By default, BGP based L3VPN use shortest path routing across the transport underlay. However, BGP based VPN traffic can also get automatically steered into SR policy, such as one created by a flexible algorithm or a point-to-point TE tunnel. This is achieved by coloring VPN routes within MP-BGP with extended community attributes. As illustrated in Figure 13-13 this can be done in two ways 1. While defining a VRF, define a color for all Prefixes associated with that VRF, or 2. When sending or receiving BGP routes, using a policy to “color” the route. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 Figure 13-13 Import / Export of route colors for SR policy selection In either case, the VPN route will now be tagged with a color and traffic for the destination will automatically get steering into an SR policy based on the color associated with the VPN route. # 14 Quality of Service in packet-switched networks
This chapter discusses the Quality of Service (QoS) capabilities that must be deployed to support the delivery of Xhaul traffic and non-Xhaul traffic in the RAN network.

## 14.1 Xhaul transport core interface QoS
For the purposes of this document, the transport network domain will be considered to be constructed of two interface types. Core interfaces and edge interfaces. An interface is considered to be transport network core if it is interconnecting two devices inside the transport domain. An interface is considered transport network edge if it is connecting to an element outside the transport domain. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 11 14.1.2 Core interface queue structure
The Xhaul domain must support a differentiated QoS architecture supporting priority queueing and scheduling with weighted fair queue scheduler for non-priority packets. [R76]: MUST support EF forwarding described in IETF RFC 3246 [66] mapped to a strict priority scheduler with shaping and policing to prevent bandwidth starvation of other classes. [R77]: MUST support AF forwarding model described in IETF RFC 2597 [51] mapped to a WFQ,

# 18 WRR or MDRR scheduler for non-priority classes.
[R78]: MUST support the ability to manipulate queue depths

# 21 14.1.2.1 Flat queue model
In the flat queue model, the TNE should support a single level of queue on each physical interface. This model is used for a single topology infrastructure, or a “soft slicing” where the QoS model for each slice is common and bandwidth is dynamically shared between slices.

# 26 Figure 14-1 Example Xhaul queue model
The system should be capable of supporting a minimum of six queues within the core domain. An example queuing model is provided in Figure 14-1which should be adapted to fit the available queue and scheduling model available in the deployed hardware. All deployments must support a strict priority queue dedicated to latency sensitive front haul traffic (shown as queue marking 5). This queue must be serviced in strict priority over all other queues up ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 to its shaped or policed limit. If the node is providing transit for G.8275.2 PTPoIP as a PTP unaware element, then PTP packets MUST also be scheduled in this queue. If the hardware supports multiple levels of strict priority queueing, and is a PTP unaware node, then PTP MAY also be scheduled in a dedicated highest priority queue to minimise packet delay variation (PDV). Two further latency sensitive queues are defined, one for network control (shown as queue marking 7) and one for other latency sensitive transit traffic (e.g. latency sensitive Backhaul or Midhaul U- plane or latency sensitive business or consumer traffic) (shown as queue marking 2). These queues should be configured to be serviced with a latency bound suitable for the traffic associated with them. The scheduling model used will be dependent on the specific HW choice. For example, this could be a guaranteed bandwidth queue with suitable scheduler weight and queue depth, or a high priority queue with lower priority scheduling than that for the latency sensitive Fronthaul traffic. Additional queues are defined for guaranteed bandwidth traffic (Management (shown as queue marking 6), guaranteed bandwidth U-plane (shown as queue marking 3,4) and best effort traffic

# 14 (shown as queue marking 0,1)).
Additional queues may be supported if the carrier deems necessary. The example queue model is show in Figure 14-1 provides example MPLS “Traffic Class” (TC) or often called EXP, based classification for the queues. It should be noted that a transport based on SRv6 allows the use of IP DSCP as the QoS marker, allowing for more flexibility in the queue model, and that more queues may be used if the marking scheme and hardware are appropriate. [R79]: MUST support a minimum of 6 HW queues per physical interface

# 22 14.1.2.2 Hierarchical queue model
The hierarchical queue model provides a capability to support a segmented infrastructure “Hard slicing” where the QoS model for each slice is different, or where each slice requires dedicated bandwidth. (see Figure 14-2 for details) Here the model the transport device must support a minimum of two levels of queue hierarchy on each physical interface. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 3 Figure 14-2 Sample hierarchical queue model
In this model the first, or child level defines the queues needed to support the capabilities associated with the slice. These might be the same as in the flat queue model or may be different. In the second or parent level, a scheduler is defined to allocate the maximum bandwidth that will be available to that hard slice. It should be noted that the sum of the guaranteed bandwidth to each shaper should not exceed the interface bandwidth. As with the flat queue model, example is provided which should be adapted for the specific HW in use. [R80]: MUST support a minimum of 6 HW queues per logical interface [R81]: MUST support a minimum of two tiers of configurable scheduler per physical interface

# 15 14.1.3 Transport network core interface marking structure
Transport nodes should preserve the QoS marking of transported frames and packets across the transport network. This should be accomplished via the use of the pipe or short pipe model described in IETF RFC2983[59]. The specific marking structure used to define the transport QoS behaviours is left to the individual providers and is dependent on the transport encapsulation implemented. An example marking structure for MPLS TC values is shown in Figure 14-1.

# 23 14.1.4 Core interface scheduling model
Latency sensitive and network control plane traffic should be forwarded using an expedited forwarding model as described in IETF RFC 3246[66]. In order to preserve minimum latency, these queues should be scheduled with a maximum of one packet in each queue and be allocated a priority forwarding schedule in the NPU. To prevent bandwidth starvation of non-priority scheduled traffic, each priority queue should be shaped or policed at a combined capacity less than the physical rate of each egress interface in the core, and with sufficient bandwidth capacity available ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 for the latency sensitive Fronthaul services they are supporting. Where needed a TSN based scheduler may also be implemented if the interface bandwidth demands such optimisation. Details on TSN may be found in section 10.1.1.2.1. Guaranteed bandwidth queues (management and best effort) should be scheduled using the assured forwarding model described in IETF RFC 2597[51]. These queues should be scheduled using a Weighted Round Robin (WRR), Minimum deficit round robin (MDRR) or weighted fair queue (WFQ) scheduler, depending on the capability available in the NPU. Where network control traffic is assigned to a guaranteed bandwidth queue, the scheduler for that queue must be configured to support minimum latency to ensure time sensitive network control traffic (eg BFD) is not delayed. The scheduler MUST have sufficient buffer capacity to avoid loss in these queues due to the effects of micro-burst caused by the aggregation of traffic from different ingress interfaces, or speed mismatch (higher to lower).

## 14.2 Xhaul transport network edge interface QoS
PE elements in the transport network domain will be responsible for providing logical separation and encapsulation for transport. It can be assumed that there are two types of traffic that will be presented for transport. 1. Ethernet frames. For example, RoE or eCPRI frames not using an IP header. 2. IP packets. For example, eCPRI packets or Backhaul traffic whose encapsulation includes an

# 19 IP header.

### 14.2.1 Transport network domain PE ingress classification of Ethernet frames.
For the purposes of this section, it is assumed that there will be a physical or logical interface attaching the Ethernet frame device to the transport network edge PE. As an example, this could be a Mobile Client, such as a Front Haul Gateway or O-DU supporting an RU using RoE. PE nodes in the transport network will perform classification on traffic ingressing the domain using different models. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 5 14.2.1.1 Untagged frames
As per Figure 14-3(1) the Mobile Client (MC) presents a flow of untagged frames to the PE. The PE uses the local port as the context for the MC. This context must be preserved in the transport network and presented at the port level (untagged) at the remote PE. Because the PE has no knowledge of the MC encapsulation model, or priority needed for each frame, all frames must be given the same appropriate treatment (and transport marking) to support the encapsulation mode. It can be assumed that the operator has this knowledge at the port level and can apply the appropriate local policy for both transport marking and PHB for all frames. These frames should be encapsulated with the appropriate transport and marked with QoS marking for carried in the class defined in section 14.1.2 for Latency sensitive Fronthaul traffic.

# 15 14.2.1.2 Tagged frames (VLAN), PCP unset or untrusted
As per Figure 14-3(2) The RoE mapper presents a flow of VLAN tagged frames to the PE. The PE uses the VLAN and local port as the context for the RoE mapper. This context must be preserved in the transport network and presented at the remote PE with the same VLAN marking. Because the PE has no knowledge of the RoE mapper encapsulation model, or priority needed for each frame, all frames must be given the same appropriate treatment and transport marking, to support the encapsulation mode. It can be assumed that the operator has this knowledge at the either the VLAN or port level and can apply the appropriate local policy for both transport marking and PHB for all frames. These frames should be encapsulated with the appropriate transport and marked with QoS marking for carried in the class defined in 14.1.2 for Latency sensitive Fronthaul traffic.

# 25 14.2.1.3 Tagged frames (VLAN), PCP set and trusted
As per Figure 14-3(3). The RoE mapper presents a flow of VLAN tagged frames to the PE. The PE uses the VLAN and local port as the context for the RoE mapper. This context must be preserved in the transport network and presented at the remote PE with the same VLAN marking. In this model it is assumed that the RoE mapper supports a differential marking scheme for flows requiring different treatment. The marking is placed in the PCP field of the VLAN header (described by IEEE 802.1p). The PE should be capable of classifying flows based on the PCP marking and implementing an appropriate PHB. The PE should also apply an appropriate marking to the frames as supported by the transport model in use. It can be assumed that the operator has this knowledge of the PCP markings from the RoE mapper. Each class presented by the RoE mapper must be mapped to one of the class markings defined in section 14.1.2. It is assumed that the operator has appropriate knowledge to determine this mapping. [R82]: MUST support classification of frames based on 802.1p PCP bit field [R83]: MUST support classification of frames based on incoming logical interface. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 [D41]: SHOULD support ingress policing using a single rate 2 color policer described in RFC2698 [52] or RFC4115 [76] [D42]: SHOULD support ingress policing using a dual rate 3 color policer described in RFC2698 [52] or RFC4115 [76] [R84]: MUST support ingress marking of frames based on result of soft policing using policers in [D41]: and [D42]:.

# 9 14.2.2 Transport domain PE ingress classification IP packets.
Unlike Ethernet frames, IP packets will always have a QoS marking field available to them. As a result, we do not have to be concerned with IP packets arriving unmarked from a QoS perspective and must simply determine if we trust the marking.

# 13 14.2.2.1 Marked packets DSCP untrusted
Similar to Figure 14-3(2). The client element presents a flow of DSCP marked packets to the PE. The PE uses local port as the context for the flow. This context must be preserved in the transport network and presented at the remote PE with the same DSCP marking. Because the PE has no knowledge of the client element encapsulation model, or priority needed for each packet, all packets must be given the same appropriate treatment and transport marking, to support the encapsulation mode. It can be assumed that the operator has this knowledge at the port level and can apply the appropriate local policy for both transport marking and PHB for all frames. These frames should be encapsulated with the appropriate transport and marked with QoS marking for carried in the class defined in section 14.1.2 for Latency sensitive Fronthaul traffic.

# 23 14.2.2.2 Marked packets DSCP trusted
Similar to Figure 14-3. The client element presents a flow of DSCP marked packets to the PE. The PE uses the local port as the context for the flow. This context must be preserved in the transport network and presented at the remote PE with the same DSCP marking. In this model it is assumed that the client element or IP source supports a differential marking scheme for flows requiring different treatment. The marking is placed in the DSCP field of the IP header. The PE should be capable of classifying flows based on the DSCP marking and implementing an appropriate PHB. The PE should also apply an appropriate marking to the frames as supported by the transport model in use. It can be assumed that the operator has this knowledge of the DSCP markings from the client element or IP source. Each class presented by the client element or IP source must be mapped to one of the class markings defined in section 14.1.2. It is assumed that the operator has appropriate knowledge to determine this mapping. [R85]: MUST support classification of frames based on IPv4 DSCP field [R86]: MUST support classification of frames based on IPv6 DSCP field ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 8 14.2.4 PE Egress scheduling
Traffic arriving at a PE from the infrastructure, to be transmitted to a CE device should be done so based on the model used for its classification on ingress.

# 11 14.2.4.1 Unclassified traffic
Where an interface is using unclassified traffic, that is; all traffic is always marked as default by the CE or traffic with no marking available e.g. ethernet without a VLAN header, traffic should be forwarded on a FIFO basis. In this model it must be ensured that the flow of traffic into the PE toward the CE MUST be at a lower rate than the interface attaching the PE to the CE to avoid congestion resulting in latency or loss.

# 18 14.2.4.2 Classified traffic
Where an interface is using classified traffic, that is traffic has a marking scheme available, and traffic is marked using this scheme, traffic should be forwarded to the CE with a queueing scheme and scheduling model that is appropriate to the traffic for that CE. The specific marking and queueing scheme are beyond the scope of this document but MUST be understood by the operator. In this model the PE MUST support the classification and queueing of the CE destined traffic based on the marking on the CE packet or frame. This is understood as “pipe model – after” as defined in IETF RFC 2983, section 5 – 6. [R87]: MUST support classification of encapsulated frames or packets based on 802.1p PCP bit field or IP DSCP field as described in IETF RFC 2983 section 5-6

## 15.1 Multicast use cases
Multicast use cases in an Xhaul transport network come from two categories as described below. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 10 15.1.2 MBMS/5MBS transport
3GPP TS 23.246 MBMS Architecture and Functional Specification (R15) and TR 23.757 Study on architectural enhancements for 5G multicast-broadcast services (5MBS, R17) all support “shared delivery method” with which multicast/broadcast traffic is transported via multicast to RAN nodes (N3/N9), who will then transmit over the air. This means multicast transport is needed to CU-UP. Another “individual delivery method” may also be used – UPFs send individual copies of multicast traffic over PDU sessions to UEs, transparent to RAN nodes. With this method, if UPFs are distributed, then multicast should be used in DNN to the UPFs (N6). Note that, a UPF may be connected to multiple DNNs as the anchored PDU sessions may belong to multiple DNNs.

# 17 Packet Switched TNE Security
Packet Switched Transport Network Equipment (TNE) plays a vital role in building the transport infrastructure needed to support a 5G infrastructure. As such the packet switched TNEs needs to support a set of security features associated with: 1) The security of the TNEs (both physical security nad user access security) 2) The security of the network control, data and management plane protocols the TNEs run 3) Security functionality required by the TNEs to support security functionality required by the 5G mobile components. This section, which deals with transport specific requirements, in association with O-

# 34 RAN.WG11.Security-Requirements-Specifications [27] provides guidelines and requirements for security features required for an O-RAN compliant packet switched transport infrastructure.

## 17.1 TNE physical security
This section describes the measures to improve the security of the TNE, when the TNE is placed in unsecured, publicly accessible location. For example, such as remote unattended site, or a shared rack with a partner or customer organization ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 30 17.1.2 Auxiliary Port
Many TNEs have as well an auxiliary port, which is intended to be used with a modem to provide dial-in access to a TNE in remote locations. In most cases, the auxiliary port can also be used as a secondary console port, in which case it inherits some console port security concerns. In most cases, the auxiliary port is not used in typical network deployments. Leaving that port enabled creates security concern. [R91]: TNE MUST provide capability to disable auxiliary port [R92]: TNE MUST provide capability to secure auxiliary port in a similar manner as console port, if the auxiliary port is used

# 42 17.1.3 USB Port
Many TNEs today have external user accessible USB ports used for booting the device off a USB stored image or for loading software onto the device’s internal storage. The USB port can be exploited to load malicious device software or used to easily transfer provider information in the case of a device with a compromised management plane. In many cases the device when booting ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 will give the user an option to boot off the USB if a capable USB storage device is connected. Leaving the USB port active creates a security concern. [R93]: TNE MUST provide capability to disable USB port

# 6 17.1.4 Front Panel functions
Many TNEs have front panel with physical buttons, LCD displays or menu options to perform system control and maintenance functions, like bringing a line-card offline or online, restoring the factory default configuration, acknowledging alarms, etc. There may be scenarios, where TNEs are placed in an unsecure location, such as remote unattended site, or a shared rack with a partner or customer organization. Such unsecure locations require enhanced security for front panel functions

# 12 (buttons, LCD displays, menus, etc.).
[R94]: TNE MUST provide capability to disable/enable front panel functions (buttons, menus, LCD displays, etc.)

# 17 17.1.5 TNE software security
Due to the security risks posed by malicious software, the TNE must validate software loaded onto the device before execution. The method for implementation is outside the scope of this document, however the signing of all software images by the TNE vendor’s private key is the common industry practice. Image signing applies to boot software as well as incremental updates applied to a running device. [D43]: TNE SHOULD validate the device boot loader before execution, halting boot on revocation [D44]: TNE SHOULD support signed boot images validated by the device boot loader before execution, halting boot on revocation [D45]: TNE SHOULD validate all software images and updates prior to execution

# 29 17.1.6 Zero Touch Provisioning
Due to the scale of today’s mobile packet switched networks, Zero Touch Provisioning (ZTP) is often used either in the field to deploy new devices or replace existing devices with hardware impairments. While ZTP operations are typically internal to a provider network, it’s important to secure the communication and components used with ZTP. RFC 8572 [144] defines Secure ZTP, a framework for ensuring the ZTP process is secure end to end. The primary points of security for

# 35 ZTP are:
1) ZTP client validation, to ensure the client is trusted by the server before offering ZTP artifacts or configuration information 2) ZTP server validation, to ensure the server is trusted by the client before accepting any ZTP configuration or artifacts 3) Artifact validation, to ensure the ZTP components downloaded from the ZTP server are trusted before being loaded or executed [R95]: TNE MUST provide follow the SZTP framework defined in RFC 8572 [144] if the device supports ZTP ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 [R96]: TNE MUST follow methods and formats defined in RFC 8366 [136] to ensure the validity of the device from the manufacturer using an Ownership Voucher

# 4 17.1.7 PXE boot over management or data ports
Many TNEs today will attempt to boot via PXE as part of their Zero Touch Provisioning process. The ZTP process can run on the management Ethernet interface as well as on standard data interfaces. This process can be a security risk if the physical device location is compromised, allowing an attacker to load malicious software onto the device or compromise its boot integrity protections. [R97]: TNE MUST provide capability to disable ZTP, if ZTP is not in use

## 17.2 TNE user access security
This section describes the measures to improve the security of the TNE, preventing unauthorized user to access the device.

# 17 17.2.1 TACACS+ Authentication
Typically, the default authentication used to authenticate user on the TNE is password authentication using locally stored user data (username, password). In large-scale deployments, like 5G Xhaul deployment, local authentication database on each TNE is very impractical. Therefore, the recommended solution is to use TACACS+ server, which should always be considered the first and principal authentication method. After integrating the TNE into TACACS+ authentication infrastructure, the TACACS+ authentication method should be preferred over password authentication using local authentication database. When user authentication order is set on TNE (with TACACS+ authentication as first, and authentication using local authentication database as second) the user is first authenticated with TACACS+ server. If TACACAS+ server responds (either granting the access or refusing the access), this response is used by the TNE to either allow or deny the user access to the device. However, if TACACS+ server doesn’t respond (is unreachable), local password authentication is used to grant or deny access to the device. Therefore, it is always recommended to have limited number of local users defined on the TNE as a last resort for authentication. These users can be used for authentication purpose in failure cases, when TACACS+ server is not available. TACACS+ provides not only user authentication, i.e., to determine who a user is, but as well authorization, i.e., to grant access rights to certain portions of the TNE, or to certain configuration or operational commands on the TNE. Additionally, TACACS+ performs accounting, which is the action of recording what a user is doing and/or has done. This is commonly known as AAA

# 39 (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting).
[R98]: TNE MUST support TACACS+ for user authentication, in accordance with Section 5 of RFC 8907: “The Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+)

# 44 Protocol” [153]
ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 [R99]: TNE MUST support TACACS+ for user authorization, in accordance with Section 6 of RFC 8907: “The Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+) Protocol” [153] [D46]: TNE SHOULD support TACACS+ for user accounting, in accordance with Section 7 of RFC 8907: “The Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+)

# 7 Protocol” [153]
[R100]: TNE MUST support specification of authentication order, preferring TACACS+ authentication (RFC 8907 [153]) over authentication using local user database

# 12 17.2.2 Login Message
Typically, by default, no message is displayed by the TNE before or after login. It is strongly advised that a system login message is present before the user logs in, as well as another message after user successfully logged in. A strongly worded login banner SHOULD include statements regarding the following:

# 17 ▪ Clear prohibition of unauthorized access.
▪ Clear prohibition of unauthorized use. This warns authorized users against unauthorized use of the system. ▪ Warning that the system may be monitored. Note that the wording might have important ramifications for successful prosecutions. Do not say the system will be monitored. ▪ Statement that there is no expectation of privacy. This statement insures that no legal defense can be mounted claiming that the company should not have monitored an unauthorized user. ▪ Statement that results of monitoring may be provided to the appropriate authorities. ▪ Statement that continued use of the system implies consent to the stated terms and conditions. ▪ Warning to log off immediately if consent is not given. Login banners SHOULD NOT include any of the following information:

# 29 ▪ Information about the device type or software

# 30 ▪ Information about the device location

# 31 ▪ Contact information

# 32 ▪ Administrator information
There could be two level of messages displayed by on TNE’s terminal: one message appearing before the user logs in, and 2nd message after the user logs in. [R101]: TNE MUST support modifiable messages displayed on the user session before and after user login ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 [D47]: Login banners SHOULD NOT include details about the device, location or contact/administrator information

# 5 17.2.3 Security Protocols
In order to provide secure user to access to TNEs for configuration management, security protocols are required that provide Confidentiality, Integrity, Authenticity and replay protection. This section provides details on Secure Shell (SSH, RFC4252, [82]) and Transport Layer Security (TLS, RFC5246, [95] and RFC8446, [140]).

# 10 17.2.3.1 Secure Shell (SSH)
Requirements for O-RAN elements supporting SSH are generally defined in the O-RAN

# 12 ALLIANCE TS: “O-RAN Security Protocols Specification” ([29]).
[D48]: TNEs supporting SSH SHOULD implement the protocol as defined in [29], clause 4.1.

# 16 17.2.3.2 Transport Layer Security (TLS)
Requirements for O-RAN elements supporting TLS are generally defined in the O-RAN

# 18 ALLIANCE TS: “O-RAN Security Protocols Specification” ([29]).
[D49]: TNEs supporting SSH SHOULD implement the protocol as defined in [29], clause 4.2.

# 22 17.2.4 Password requirements
Variety of requirements can be used to strengthen passwords for greater security. TNE should provide a framework allowing to enforce password rules defined by the operator to conform to a particular set of requirements defined in operator’s security policy. These password rules may include such things as length, number of changes, type of characters, numbers, or letters, case, etc. [D50]: TNE SHOULD support definition and enforcement of user password rules like length, number of changes, type of characters, numbers, or letters, case, etc.

# 30 17.2.5 Device lockout
Malicious users sometimes might try to log in to a secure TNE by guessing an authorized user account’s password. Locking out a user account after several failed authentication attempts helps protect the device from malicious users. [D51]: TNE SHOULD have the possibility to lockout the user after a number of failed attempts, and to set the amount of time before the user can attempt to log in to the device again.

## 17.3 Transport Network control plane security

# 38 17.3.1 Control plane DoS/DDoS protection
A denial-of-service (DoS) attack against an TNE is any attempt to disturb legitimate traffic or deny valid users access the TNE by using up all the resources of the TNE. Distributed denial-of-service ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 (DDoS) attacks involve an attack from multiple sources, enabling a much greater amount of traffic to attack the TNE. The attacks typically use network protocol control packets to trigger a large number of exceptions, which are packets handed over from the data plane to the control plane of the TNE. This results in an excessive processing load that disrupts normal network operations. TNE MUST have DDoS protection capability, which enables the TNE to continue functioning while under an attack. It identifies and suppresses malicious control packets while enabling legitimate control traffic to be processed. TNE SHOULD have possibility to customize DDoS protection profiles allowing to optimize DDoS protection of network control traffic in a particular deployment. To protect against DDoS attacks, typically filters and policers for host-bound exception traffic are used. The filters completely block specific types of control traffic (for example, if OSPF is not used in particular deployment, there is no need to send OSPF packets to the TNE’s control plane), while policers specify rate limits for individual types of protocol control packets or for all control packet types for a protocol. Control traffic is dropped when it exceeds policer values. Each violation SHOULD immediately generates a notification to alert operators about a possible attack. The violation SHOULD be counted, the time that the violation starts noted, and the time of the last observed violation noted. [R102]: TNE MUST support protection mechanisms (filters, policer) to protect own control plane from DoS/DDoS attacks [D52]: TNE SHOULD have the possibility to customize DoS/DDoS protection parameters to protect own control plane [D53]: TNE SHOULD have the possibility to raise alarms, when DoS/DDoS attacks are detected

# 29 17.3.2 Control plane protocols protection
Transport control plane uses various protocols to exchange information between TNEs. This information is required to build paths across transport network, exchange label information (in MPLS deployments), exchange service information (L3VPN, L2VPN), monitor the network state (periodic OAM messages), and more (for example, determine the virtual gateway state in multi- homed environment). These protocols could be divided into following groups:

# 35 ▪ IGP (e.g., OSPFv2, OSPFv3, IS-IS)

# 36 ▪ Multicast (e.g., PIM, MSDP)
▪ Protocols to distribute transport labels (e.g. LDP, RSVP)

# 38 ▪ Other protocols (e.g. BFD, VRRP, …)
This document doesn’t mandate any specific protocol to be used. For example, one deployment could use OSPFv2 as the IGP, while other deployment could use IS-IS as the IGP. However, if certain protocol is used, this document mandates minimum security requirements for each protocol that must be fulfilled. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 15 Generic Cryptographic Authentication” [103]

# 17 17.3.2.1 OSPFv2
OSPFv2 has built-in authentication mechanism defined in RFC 2328: “OSPF Version 2” [47]. It defines three authentication types:

# 20 ▪ 0: Null authentication

# 21 ▪ 1: Simple password

# 22 ▪ 2: Cryptographic authentication
Null (no authentication) and simple (clear text) authentication methods are not sufficient in today’s network. [R104]: In deployments using OSPFv2, TNE MUST support cryptographic authentication in accordance with RFC 2328: “OSPF Version 2” [47].

# 28 17.3.2.2 OSPFv3
OSPF version 3 (OSPFv3), unlike OSPF version 2, does not have a built-in authentication method and relies on IPsec to provide this functionality. This authentication functionality for OSPFv3 is defined in RFC 4552: “Authentication/Confidentiality for OSPFv3” [84]. [R105]: In deployments using OSPFv3, TNE MUST support IPsec based authentication for OSPFv3 packets in accordance with RFC 4552: “Authentication/Confidentiality for

# 35 OSPFv3” [84]

# 36 17.3.2.3 BGP
BGP is TCP based protocol, therefore it benefits from RFC 5925: “The TCP Authentication Option” (TCP-AO) [113] to protect against the malicious or accidental insertion of unauthorized BGP data into the network by preventing the establishment of BGP adjacencies with any unauthenticated router. As per [113] TCP-AO specifies the use of stronger Message Authentication Codes (MACs), protects against replays even for long-lived TCP connections, and provides more details on the association of security with TCP connections than TCP MD5 introduced in the BGP specification [79]. Further, TCP-AO uses cryptographic algorithms to compute the MAC that is ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 used to authenticate a segment and its headers. MAC algorithms are specified in a separate RFC 5926: “Cryptographic Algorithms for the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO)” [114]. This allows updating the algorithm requirements independently from the protocol. [R106]: TNE MUST support the TCP Authentication Option Authentication to secure BGP sessions in accordance with RFC 5925: “The TCP Authentication Option Authentication” [113] [R107]: TNE MUST support HMAC-SHA-1-96 MAC algorithm for TCP-AO in accordance with RFC 5926: “Cryptographic Algorithms for the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO)” [114] [D54]: TNE SHOULD support AES-128-CMAC-96 MAC algorithm for TCP-AO in accordance with RFC 5926: “Cryptographic Algorithms for the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO)” [114]

# 16 17.3.2.4 LDP
LDP, similarly to BGP, uses TCP for underlay transport. Therefore, TCP-AO [113] applies to LDP as well. [R108]: In deployments using LDP, TNE MUST support the TCP Authentication Option Authentication to secure LDP sessions in accordance with RFC 5925: “The TCP

# 22 Authentication Option Authentication” [113]

# 24 17.3.2.1 RSVP
IETF defined authentication for RSVP using MD5 one-way hashes in RFC 2747: “RSVP Cryptographic Authentication” [54]. RSVP protocol exchanges can be authenticated to guarantee that only trusted neighbors participate in setting up reservations. RSVP authentication uses an HMAC MD5 message-based digest. This scheme produces a message digest based on a secret authentication key and the message contents. Small error correction to RFC 2547 [54] was provided via RFC 3097 “RSVP Cryptographic Authentication—Updated Message Type Value” [62]. IETF didn’t specified, so far, any more modern authentication method for RSVP. [R109]: In deployments using RSVP, TNE MUST support MD5-based cryptographic authentication to secure RSVP sessions in accordance with RFC 2747: “RSVP

# 37 Cryptographic Authentication” [54]
[R110]: In deployments using RSVP, TNE MUST support amendment to the cryptographic authentication in accordance with RFC 3097 “RSVP Cryptographic Authentication—

# 41 Updated Message Type Value” [62].

### 17.4.2 Certificate management for TNEs providing Open Fronthaul transport

# 4 17.4.2.1 Trust anchor provisioning
Before a TNE can establish a mutual EAP-TLS connection with a signaling peer, e.g., with an IEEE 802.1X supplicant, a TNE needs to be able to trace the peer’s certificate path to a valid trust anchor. To validate against a trust anchor, the TNE shall be able to be provisioned with one or more trust anchor certificates. The TNE shall ensure that all trust anchor certificates are stored in reset persistent memory and protected from external modification. The TNE shall be able to be provisioned with new trust anchors. The TNE shall be able to have an existing trust anchor replaced, e.g., because it has expired. The TNE should support ietf-truststore YANG model ([180]) to enable to recover the list of provisioned trust anchors and associated public keys. The present document defines the use of Certification Management Protocol version 2 (CMPv2, [78]) Initialization Response message to allow the discovered Certification Authority (CA) and Registration Authority (RA) server to provision a trust anchor.
> NOTE: The CA/RA Server identity is configured manually or by the DHCP server using
techniques described in section 17.4.2.2. The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server is not considered by the TNE as a trusted source of security bootstrapping data. When shipped, a TNE only trusts information that is signed or encrypted using a certificate chain leading to a pre-loaded trust anchor.

# 27 17.4.2.2 Operator-signed certificate enrolment

# A TNE shall support certificate enrolment using CMPv2 ([78]). Reachability (IP address, Fully
Qualified Domain Name – FQDN) to the CA/RA servers can be configured on TNE during initial TNE provisioning. Alternatively, 3GPP TS 32.509 ([7]), clause 4.2.2, specifies how the TNE supporting certificate enrolment over IPv4 can be configured with the IP address or FQDN of one or more CA/RA servers using DHCP Option 43. The DHCP Options specified in 3GPP TS 32.509 ([7]), do not specify how to signal a CA/RA server identity using DHCP for IPv6 hosts (DHCPv6). Hence, TNE certificate enrolment using CMPv2 over IPv6 shall support the signaling of vendor specific options using DHCPv6 option 17. The format of the DHCPv6 option 17 follows the format of the DHCP for IPv4 hosts (DHCPv4) encoding as specified in clause 4.2.2 of 3GPP TS 32.509 ([7]), with the additional inclusion of an Enterprise Number prior to the Type-Length-Value (TLV) option data. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) allocated private enterprise number to be used with DHCPv6 option 17 shall be 53148 (as allocated by IANA to O-RAN Alliance). 3GPP has since published 3GPP TS 28.316 ([3]), which now specifies how to signal a CA/RA server identity with DHCPv6 option 17 messages using the 3GPP registered IANA Enterprise Number (10415). The DHCP Options defined in [7] are a subset of those defined in [3]. An operator and vendor can agree to use the 3GPP registered IANA Enterprise Number in DHCPv6 messages ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 that signal the CA/RA server information instead of the O-RAN registered IANA Enterprise

# A TNE shall report any discovered multi-vendor plug-and-play servers using the o-ran-dhcp YANG
model (reference needed).

# 19 17.4.2.3 CMPv2 based certificate enrolment
This section covers the use case where a TNE is configured with the identity of a CMPv2 capable CA/RA server that the operator uses for certificate enrolment. The TNE shall attempt to enroll in the operator-PKI and may be issued an operator-signed certificate. Clause 9 of 3GPP TS 33.310 ([8]) specifies the use of CMPv2 used by base stations to obtain an operator-signed certificate using a secured communication based on the vendor-signed certificate in the base station and a vendor root certificate pre-installed in the CA/RA server. While the approach has been defined for provisioning certificates on base stations for use in either IPSec or TLS, the same techniques defined for provisioning TLS certificates on base stations can be used for provisioning TLS certificates on TNEs. The handling of certificates, including certificate profiles, shall follow the rules defined in 3GPP TS

# 32 33.310 ([8]) for TLS CA certificates. In addition:
- when a TNE generates a certificate signing request it shall populate the Subject Distinguished Name field
with a string that includes the TNE manufacturer’s name, model and serial number. The exact Subject DN sub-field used is defined in the operator of the CA/RA server’s certificate policy.
> NOTE 1: In future, an O-RAN defined certificate policy may be defined to normalize the sub-
field definition across the O-RAN ecosystem.
> NOTE 2: There are various characters that may not be permissible in the Subject Distinguished
Name Field, e.g., ":" (colon, hexadecimal character 0x34), "." (period, hexadecimal character 0x2E), "_" (underscore, hexadecimal character 0x5F), "#" (hash, hexadecimal 0x23), "£" (pound, hexadecimal 0xa3), "*" (asterisk, hexadecimal 0x2a) or "”" (double quote, hexadecimal 0x22). Manufacturers that include such characters in their name, model and/or serial number should ensure such characters are removed before including in the Subject Distinguished Name Field. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00
- when transferring messages to the CA/RA server, the TNE shall use the "port number of the CA/RA
server" and the “path to the CA/RA directory” as signalled using the DHCP options as specified in clause 4.2.2 of 3GPP TS 32.509 ([7]). If no DHCP based configuration is received by a TNE, the TNE shall use the default port 443 and default directory "/pkix/".
- The CA/RA server shall include the trust anchor for the operator issued certificate and the appropriate
certificate chains in the initialization response message.
- The TNE shall store the operator issued certificate and corresponding certificate chain in reset persistent
memory. When configured to operate with EAP-TLS, a TNE that has a valid certificate issued by an operator PKI shall use this certificate to establish a mutually authenticated EAP-TLS connection for IEEE 802.1X-2020 [39] authentication.

# 12 17.4.2.4 Operation with vendor-signed certificates
All TNEs should be pre-provisioned at a factory with a unique device vendor-signed certificate and its entire certificate chain up to the root. If a TNE fails to enroll in an operator-PKI, as specified in section 17.4.2.2, a TNE configured to operate with TLS may use its vendor-signed certificate initially. The vendor’s public trusted certificate and certificate management services should be accessible within the operator network to allow management of vendor-signed certificates. The extended use of unmanaged vendor-signed certificates, such as outside of enrolment, is not recommended.

# 18 5G Slicing in a packet switched Xhaul network
Network Slicing is end-to-end partitioning of the network resources and network functions so that selected applications/services/connections may run in isolation from each other for a specific business purpose. The overall slicing architecture is shown in Figure 18-1 and covers the orchestration infrastructure and at the physical layer can cover the radio access network, the mobile core, including data centers and virtualization aspects, and the X-haul transport network.

# 29 Figure 18-1: Overall 5G slicing architecture
ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 Although slicing is a key capability of 5G, there is debate as to how it exactly translates into the transport network, which mobile interfaces (Fronthaul, Midhaul, Backhaul, N6) need to be sliced, what form they will take, and the number of slices required at the transport layer. For the purposes of this document the Xhaul transport infrastructure needs the capability to support transport requirements of the: 1. O-RAN and 3GPP control, management, and user plane interfaces.

# 8 2. Wireline consumer, enterprise, and wholesale services.
This includes 5G transport slicing, which from a mobile perspective may include:

# 11 1. Transport separation between Fronthaul, Midhaul, Backhaul interfaces.
2. Transport separation between Control, management, and user plane interfaces of each domain. 3. The characteristics of a transport slice are defined in clause 5.2.3 of 3GPP Technical Report 22.891. Although not referenceable, further useful information can be found in various expired personal informational IETF drafts which provide thinking on the characteristics of a sliced transport network. Some of the key points are: ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00
