o Performance o Operational o Security o Reliability

# 13 • Abstraction
o Virtualization of network functions (where appropriate) o Use of shared compute resources In the transport space, the informal terms, hard and soft slicing has emerged. This refers to the level of isolation between different slices. In both cases they need to support the functions outlined above but the way the slice is built and managed differs considerably.
- Hard slicing: Transport resources are dedicated to a specific “Network Slice Instance” (NSI).
In this case a resource is dedicated to a particular slice and not available to other slices.
- Soft slicing: The transport slice has the characteristics outlined above but a resource is shared
and can be re-used by other slice instances. A packet switched infrastructure, as described in this document, has an extensive toolset, consisting of underlay forwarding solutions, Quality of Service (QoS) and VPNs that allows an operator to scalable partition the transport network to cater for both hard and soft slices use cases. Figure 18-3 outlines some of the packet switched features that can be flexibly combined to create transport slice with different level of resource sharing. Figure 18-3: Packet switched toolset for transport level slicing ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 When considering hard and soft slices it is important to bear in mind they should be thought of as a spectrum of capability, rather than one or the other.

## 18.1 Packet-switched underlay network
The packet-switched underlay network can use MPLS, SRv6 or a combination.

# 6 18.1.1 Underlay transport plane
The transport plane determines how traffic is sent over the packet-switched underlay infrastructure. Four approaches are outlined for constructing the underlay transport plane/planes for a 5G transport infrastructure. In each of the first three cases the level of resource sharing reduces, hence the slice solution becomes harder in nature but may introduces scalability and operational challenges. Fourth mapping approach is based on 5QI/DSCP, and scaling doesn’t depend on the number of slices.

# 12 18.1.2 Single transport plane for all slices
The underlay network relies solely on the routing protocols (IGPs and EGPs) to calculate a single forwarding table based on shortest path routing. The routing protocol sees all links and there is a single forwarding table based on IGP and BGP metrics. All traffic takes the shortest path between two points within the network and utilises ECMP. In the context of slicing, all slices will see the same set of paths between end points within the network. It can be considered the softest slicing solution in terms of the underlay transport plane. However, although the infrastructure is shared between slices, it is highly scalable, widely implemented in 4G and critical enterprise environments, and is capable of delivering high quality

# 21 SLAs.

# 22 18.1.3 Transport plane per 5G service type
Within the underlay network multiple transport planes are built to meet the specific forwarding behaviors associated with the different 5G services types. One or more customers can then use these transport planes. This is achieved using VPNs and traffic steering techniques. The transport planes can utilise different topologies and be optimized based on different criteria. For example, a URLLC service types could be optimised to use only the most reliable links in the network and select the best paths between endpoints based on link delay metrics. In contrast, the eMBB service types could be designed to use cheap, high bandwidth links, based on paths calculated with IGP metrics correlated with link capacity (high link capacity → low IGP metric). And, NB-IoT service types, which don’t require neither low latency communication, nor high capacity, could use a 3rd transport plane with paths established based on TE metrics, favoring links for this type of services. This concept is outlined in Figure 18-4. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 Transport Plane is a group of paths (tunnels) with common optimization strategy (topology constraints, metric type, …) Automatic mapping Prefix: eMBB1 Prefix: eMBB2 Prefix: URLLC2 between service prefix Tunnel types: Flex-Algo, RSVP-TE, SR-TE, SRv6-TE, BGP-CT VPN Label: V1 VPN Label: V2 VPN Label: V6 and underlay transport PNH: PE1 PNH: PE1 PNH: PE1 VRF Import based on RT RT: VPN01 RT: VPN02 RT: VPN06 planebased on Color Mapping based on Color: 1 Color: 1 Color: 3 Extended Community Color VPN O-CU eMBB O-DU VPN01 T P r la a n n e s p X ort Color: 1 VPN O-CU services O-DU VPN02 Color: 1 Color: 1 PE1 NB-IoT O-DU VPN03 Transport Color: 2 Plane Y services O-DU VPN04 Color: 2 Color: 2 VPN O-CU URLLC O-DU VPN05 Transport Color: 3 VPN O-CU services O-DU VPN06 C Pl o a l n or e : 3 Z Color: PE3 VPN O-CU PE2 VPN O-CU PE4 Figure 18-4: Transport Plane per 5G service type – midhaul example To implement such an approach, a mix of shortest path routing and traffic engineering solutions could be used. Traffic engineering options include flex-algo, SR-TE or traditional MPLS TE. As with any traffic engineering approach, consideration needs to be made of scale and state held within the network. Perhaps the simplest approach would be to use the default Flex-algorithm for eMBB and the mMTC services and a delay optimized flexible algorithm for the URLLC services. Backbone links and even nodes could be considered for inclusion or exclusion into the delay optimized flex-algorithm transport planes based on whether the algorithm is enabled on a TNE and

# 11 TE affinities associated with the links.
The mapping between services and transport planes can be simplified with the usage of Color Extended Community defined in RFC 5512 [100]. Each transport plane (each tunnel being part of specific transport plane) is associated with some color value. For example, latency optimized tunnels use color 1 (Transport Plane A), capacity optimized tunnels use color 2 (Transport Plane B), and remaining tunnels use color 3 (Transport Plane C). At the same time, service prefixes are advertised via BGP with appropriate Color Extended Community. URLLC service prefixes use community value 1, eMBB service prefixes community value 2, and NB-IoT service prefixes community 3. On the PE router receiving such service prefixes, selection of appropriate transport plane is automatic based on matching colors advertised via Color Extended Community with the service prefix and the color associated with the transport plane.

# 23 18.1.4 Transport plane per slice customer
This is a variation on the previous scheme. In this case rather than a transport plane per 5G service type, a transport plane for individual customers is defined, as depicted in Figure 18-5. The same techniques outlined above would be used but very careful consideration needs to be given to scale and operational complexity of such an approach. In this case, scalability is a function of the number of customers using the network rather than the 5G service types. # 7 18.1.5 Transport plane per 5QI group (5QI-aware mapping)
5G slices might carry traffic belonging to multiple 5QI flows. Annex F: Transport network slicing solution for WG1 Slicing (informational) proposes an approach for mapping between 5QI and DSCP, and for grouping multiple 5QI/DSCP flows to limited number of 5QI/DSCP groups, where each group contains 5QI/DSCP flows (from multiple slices) with similar characteristics. This grouping is introduced to allow easy mapping of large number of 5QIs to limited set of transport resources, like for example queues in TNEs. 5QI/DSCP grouping allows as well for intelligent transport plane mapping, as outlined in Figure 18-6. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 Figure 18-6: Transport Plane per 5QI group (5QI-aware mapping) – midhaul example In this example, three 5QI groups (group X: DCSP A; group Y: DSCP B, D; group Z: DSCP C, E, F) are uniquely mapped to three transport planes. With this approach, Color Extended Community is no longer used, as the mapping is based on DSCP (which corresponds to some 5QI). 5QI-aware mapping is most advanced mapping option between the service flows and underlay transport planes.

## 18.2 Quality of Service
Quality of Service is an important component in slicing a transport infrastructure. As with the transport plane, different approaches could be taken depending on the level of isolation required between slices. In considering QoS it is necessary to look at the edge QoS solution and the core QoS solutions. For more info on QoS refer to section 14 and 24.

# 15 18.2.1 Edge QoS
Edge interfaces to packet transport networks are generally the slowest and also where congestion and packet drop most often occurs. Regardless of the QoS structures implemented in the transport core, it is important with slicing to support edge conditioning of traffic on ingress and scheduling on egress to the transport network. This ensures that each slice gets its contracted overall bandwidth and class bandwidth as it enters and leaves the transport network. When slices are presented via VLANs from the mobile clients, the PE router needs a hierarchical QoS capability that can account for the overall contracted bandwidth at the VLAN level and also the overall contracted class bandwidth within the VLAN.

# 25 18.2.2 Core QoS

# 21 18.2.2.2 Dedicated queue architecture
This approach uses the same Diffserv QoS architecture, except one or more PHBs is exclusively dedicated to a particular slice or slice type. An example could be a high priority PHB, which is dedicated exclusively to the URLLC slice. At the same time other slices can share the remaining PHBs. Given the small numbers of queues normally provisioned in the core (and available traffic classes in an MPLS environment), this type of solution needs to be used with extreme care, however it is a model used today successfully in production networks to support private line services which run in a dedicated high priority queue, while simultaneously supporting other services using a shared queue architecture.

# 31 18.2.2.3 Dedicated links and queues per slice
This QoS approach achieves hard slicing by either dedicating core links or parts of a core link to a specific slice. This can be achieved by one of the following approaches:
- Using dedicated links per slice in the transport network. This could be done using full
physical Ethernet interfaces or using Ethernet TDM technology, such as flexE, to create dedicated Ethernet channels for different slices. Within these links, class-based queuing would be used to support different traffic types associated with the slice. This approach offers no ability to share unused bandwidth between slices as the links are hard partitioned.
- Using hierarchically scheduled bandwidth on core links. In this case core links would be split
using a shaper to govern the level of bandwidth available to each slice, with class-based queuing within the shaped bandwidth. This approach does offer the ability to share unused bandwidth between slices. In addition to dividing the core bandwidth up, mechanisms are required to guide slice traffic into the links or shaped bandwidth associated with each slice. Slice traffic could be guided into the appropriate links using a TE solution, such as flex-algo or SR-TE or alternatively the core routers ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 could be enhanced to schedule on a slice identifier within the packet. At this time there is discussion on this subject but as yet nothing solid. Like with the previous example, this could support a small number of slices but scaling up would be highly problematic with core provisioning, as well as edge provisioning required when a slice is defined, changed or deleted. It is also a large departure in the way QoS in core of packet networks has been managed in the past.

## 18.3 5G Services and slices
MP-BGP based L2 EVPN and L3VPNs are used to create slice instances. VPNs are very scalable in terms of numbers and endpoints and allow different flexible connectivity models. This means slices could be based on 5G service, customer or a combination of the two. Each slice would have a VPN associated with it. By default, VPNs use the default IGP based forwarding tables to forward traffic. However, VPN traffic can be directed, either by configuration or using automated traffic steering techniques based on BGP “color extended community attribute” to use traffic engineered paths. In this way, a URLLC slice could be directed to use a delay optimised TE solution. Further control of the transport level connectivity within the VPN can be achieved using Route Target filtering. For example, “Route Target” filtering could be used to stop transport level connectivity between UPFs of different customers but allow O-CUs to communicate with any UPF.

# 19 Energy efficiency in the context of Xhaul Packet
Switched Transport Network Equipments Energy efficiency is becoming relevant as sustainability goal in the operation of any kind of network, and in consequence, also for the purpose of Xhaul. The O-RAN Alliance has already setup activities in regards energy efficiency in WG5 and WG10, in relation to the management of the energy consumption at the radio level, enabled by e.g. the possibility of handling “sleep modes” of radio elements. This work is complementary to that by focusing on the transport side, specifically on which relates to packet switches solutions, as part of the scope of WG9. When dealing with Transport Network Equipments (TNEs), different approaches can be considered:

# 31 • Actions taken at architectural level

# 32 • Actions taken at transport network (TN) level
- Actions taken at Transport Network Equipment (TNE) level
The following sections elaborate on each of those approaches.

## 19.1 Architecture level
Here the purpose is the identification of actions that can positively influence the consumption of energy of the Xhaul segment at architectural level. This means the identification of architectural propositions resulting more efficient from an energy consumption perspective. This is much related to the design of the overall Xhaul solution by leveraging on architectural approaches in the direction of reducing the number of elements present in the network. Actions that could lay on this set are for instance: ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00
- Topological optimizations by concentrating the number of TNEs aggregating O-RU’s, O-
DU’s and O-CU’s, while keeping the necessary redundancy levels to satisfy service SLAs.
- On scenarios requiring both packet-switched TNEs and an underlay optical network,
schemes favouring the reduction of elements such as IPoDWDM solutions (i.e., the support of coloured interfaces on routers to avoid transponders).
- When feasible, the support of coloured interfaces directly on O-RU’s, O-DU’s and O-CU’s.
Any of these actions require an initial planning or a migration process. There could be structural dependencies on the suitability of these approaches based on the architecture design of the operators in their actual aggregation networks.

## 19.2 Transport Network (TN) level
Here the purpose is to improve the energy consumption of a network by implementing mechanisms that can dynamically optimize such consumption according to network status and conditions. Some events need to be identified as triggers for such optimization, that could require of smart management and control capabilities to make the network adapt to the observed circumstances, while reducing energy. Actions that could lay on this set are for instance:
- Concentration of traffic flows in some links during low-activity periods, then freeing up
some of the links for reducing the consumption on the corresponding TNEs. This could be done by the transport network in an isolated manner, or as part of a combined radio- transport optimization scenario. Note that additional capabilities are needed at device level for taking advantage of the links becoming empty as consequence of the traffic consolidation.
- Exposure of energy per path or topology based on the consumption of the participating
individual devices, so that upper management systems can build an overall view of the energy consumption map for taking decisions (e.g., function placement, traffic consolidation as before, etc). These actions leverage on the capability of the management system to collect the necessary information, decide on top of the collected data, and enforce control actions on the network all in an automated manner, ensuring prompting reaction to observed and even predicted network status.

## 19.3 Transport Network Equipment (TNE) level
Here the objective is to leverage on intrinsic capabilities of the TNEs for reducing its individual energy consumption under conditions that can be triggered either internally or externally (i.e., from the management systems referred before). Actions that could lay on this set are for instance:
- Presence of native capabilities for supporting “sleep modes” of operation, that is, reducing
the consumption during periods of time according to e.g. traffic patterns.
- Possibility of switching off TNE parts, especially for modular architectures, in situations
where those parts do not participate of the communications. This could be simply because there is no active participation, or because the consolidation of network traffic as described in 19.2. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 These actions leverage on the capabilities of each device, so are dependent of the particular implementations for equipment vendors. There is also a great dependency on the capabilities of the installed base, so brownfield scenarios can be no such efficient as new deployments.

# 6 19.3.1 TNE hardware design
Based on the hardware structure, TNEs can be grouped into two main categories

# 10 ▪ fixed systems

# 11 ▪ modular chassis
Fixed systems (Figure 19-1) are typically 1 RU or 2 RU devices, which do not have replacable network modules. Modular chassis (Figure 19-2), on the other hand, are typically bigger devices, with flexible hardware options (line cards, modules). This allows assembling the TNE with interfaces specifically required for the particular deployment. Fixed systems, while less flexible, when it comes to port type variations, due to their simpler hardware structure, are typically more power efficient compared to modular chassis. - Flexible, fully programmable versus fixed pipeline PFE chipsets
PFE chipsets can be divided into two main categories: flexible, fully programmable (1), and fixed pipeline, with limited programmability (2). Fixed pipeline chipsets consume less energy (Figure 19-7), as their design is simpler – they are designed to perform pre- determined functions (for example, to do the MPLS switching) with limited flexibility to program other functions (for example, perform SRv6 encapsulation/decapsulation, if the chipset was not designed from day one to perform this function). Therefore, to support particular throughput, they require less transistors comparing to flexible, fully programmable chipsets. This results in lower energy consumption. However, the tradeoff is feature flexibility offered by flexible, fully programmable PFE chipsets.

# 15 Figure 19-7: PFE chipset evolution
[D61]: To optimize PFE energy consumption, it is recommended TNE is built using fixed pipeline PFE chipsets.

# 20 • PFE chipset generations
Newer generation of chipsets, produced with 16 nm, or 7 nm (and emerging 5 nm) technologies consume significantly less energy (Figure 19-7) compared to older generation chipsets (28nm – 65nm). [D62]: To optimize PFE energy consumption, it is recommended TNE is build using new generation (<16 nm) PFE chipsets.

# 30 • Traffic Load
Traffic load might impact TNE energy consumption by about 10%-20% (TNE with minimal traffic load, versus TNE with maximal traffic load). Thus, minimizing traffic load might bring some energy savings. Some exemplary techniques to minimize traffic load are:
- Use efficient transport encapsulation with small overhead (for example, MPLS
overhead is typically smaller than SRv6 overhead) st 1 G en F le x nd 2 G ib le en (fu rd 3 lly p G en r o g ra m th 4 m G en a b le ) c th 5 G en h ip s e t a r c h th 6 ite G c en t u r e st 1 G en nd 2 G en F ix e d p ip rd 3 G en e lin e c h ip s th 4 G en e t a r c h ite c t u th 5 r e G en ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00
- Compress data before transmission, where possible and applicable (for example, photos
and videos might be resized and compressed by the application server, before they are sent to the user equipment). However, this might increase energy consumption by servers hosting applications.
- Cache frequently used data close to end-users (for example, web cache)
- Use optimized multicast replication for multicast streams (for example, IPTV
distribution via optimized multicast tree instead of ingress replication)

# 20 19.3.6 Switching fabric energy optimization
Switching fabric complex contains fabric ASICs, and SerDes complexes interconnecting fabric ASICs with PFEs (Figure 19-2). Therefore, in fabric complex, energy could be saved by switching off fabric ASICs or fabric SerDes complexes. There are couple of possible options for switch fabric design, when it comes to fabric redundancy in modular chassis. One of the common switching fabric redundancy designs is N+1 redundancy, where ‘N’ fabric interface boards provide capacity sufficient to interconnect all PFEs, and there is +1 fabric interface board as spare. For example, if the node has 8 PFEs, each PFE with 500 Gbps, the required switching fabric capacity is 4 Tbps. If the capacity of single fabric ASICs is 500 Gbps, and single fabric interface board hosts two fabric ASIC (1 Tbps per FIB), equipping the node with 5 fabric interface boards (5 Tbps in total) would provide N+1 switching fabric redundancy. In case of single fabric interface board failure, the switching fabric is still able to provide full required capacity of 4 Tbps. However, when two fabric interface boards fail, the maximum fabric capacity is reduced to 3 Tbps only. In order to provide protection for two fabric interface boards failures, N+2 (two “spare” fabric interface boards) redundancy mode would be required. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 [D67]: TNE SHOULD automatically shut down SerDes between fabric and PFE, if corresponding LC slot is empty (line card not inserted), or LC/PFE is powered off (Figure 19-10). This process SHOULD not impact other LCs or PFEs.

# 7 Figure 19-10: Fabric SerDes energy optimization
Often the TNE doesn’t operate at its full possible capacity. Some line cards or PFEs could be switched off. Some ports might be set to unused state, or not all ports might be populated with pluggable optical module. Therefore, very often the full switching fabric capacity is not required. In such situation, to maintain N+1 switching fabric redundancy, it is sufficient to take into consideration capacity requirements for PFE with highest capacity requirement (Figure 19-11).

# 20 Supporting mobile scenarios on a packet switched Xhaul
network What is clear in discussions with operators is that although section 8 outlines individual use cases, operator’s expect multiple use cases to be present in their transport network based on the need to support 4G and 5G, maturity and timelines of the O-RAN specifications, vendor product readiness, use cases and latency requirements. Figure 20-1, an adapted operator’s view, illustrates this well with multiple 4G/5G architectures present along with Enterprise and consumer services. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 Figure 20-1: An adapted O-RAN operator’s view of mobile component placement In order to make this document generic to operators, simplification is required. For this reason, the following physical topology and underlay transport solution is used as a baseline. Operators can then use the information and customize to their specific requirements.

## 20.1 Physical network
Figure 20-2 illustrates physical network layout for a metro network and its connectivity to the transport core. It consists of: 1. A collection of metro networks surrounding a transport core. Each metro network consists of a number of access networks that are consolidated by an aggregation network towards to the transport core. 2. All sites which interface to customer or mobile components supports Provider Edge functionality for L2 and L3 overlay services. 3. Data centers or location for positioning mobile components potentially exist at the hub sites, edge sites and in centralised locations. 4. Connectivity between routers is provided by line-rate point-to-point Ethernet connections derived from dark fibre or WDM. 5. Access networks could be based on either small rings, star, chained or hub and spoke topologies. To simplify the following discussion, it is assumed each cell site has a CSR connected via a single high-capacity dark fibre to the HSR in a star topology. Refer to section 10 for more details on potential fiber access topologies. 6. The Aggregation network originates from the HSR and is based on either a ring or a hub and spoke topology. For some scenarios the aggregation network may be split into a pre- aggregation and aggregation component. In this case, there is an intermediate layer of packet switches and an additional layer of statistical multiplexing. (See greyed out router / switch in

# 26 Figure 20-2)
ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 3 Figure 20-2: An example physical architecture

## 20.2 Logical underlay architecture
The logical underlay is illustrated in Figure 20-3 and consists of QoS enabled infrastructure that either uses an IP/MPLS or an SRv6 underlay data and control plane. It provides any-to-any connectivity between TNEs in the network, regardless of whether they reside in the same metro network, a different metro network or the transport core and supports both shortest path routing and traffic engineering. The underlay data planes, control plane and scaling mechanisms to enable this for IP/MPLS and SRv6 are different and discussed in their respective chapters. Both solutions have the capabilities to support best effort and traffic engineered forwarding and the capability to create discrete constrained based topologies using either traditional traffic engineering or flexible algorithm which can be optimized on criteria such as shortest path, delay and bandwidth. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 3 Figure 20-3: An example logical architecture

# 4 20.2.1 Underlay Quality of Service (QoS)
Refer to section 14 for fuller discussion on QoS. Underlay QoS refers to the scheduling used on the core or backbone links. All backbone links are enabled with a combination of priority and class- based queueing. Assignment of traffic to different queues within the core is based on marking within the packet header. In an MPLS backbone this is based on the EXP bits or traffic class field, a three-bit field, giving a maximum number of core behaviours of eight. In an IPv6 backbone this is based on the DSCP bits, a six-bit field, giving a maximum number of 64 markings and potential behaviours.

# 15 Figure 20-4: Example Xhaul queue structure
ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

## 20.3 Service architecture
For mobile services it is proposed to use BGP based VPNs to overlay service functionality onto the underlay transport network as described in section 13.
> NOTE: There is no reason this same transport infrastructure cannot support other VPN solutions
such as VXLAN or SD-WAN type solutions. All PEs and DCIs (which are also PEs) should be capable of supporting point to point Ethernet services using EVPN VPWS services and L3 BGP VPN services described in section 13. With these two basic service overlays all the scenarios outlined in section 8 can be accommodated.

# 11 20.3.1 Automated VPN Traffic Steering
If required traffic from different VPNs or specific flows within an VPN can be steered into different underlay transport planes based on coloring the MP-BGP VPN routes associated with L2 and L3VPNs. This capability is described in Annex C: MP-BGP based L3VPNs .

## 20.4 Mobile services
There are many ways Fronthaul, Midhaul and Backhaul services could be provisioned onto the transport network. Below are a set of assumptions and mechanisms used to illustrate how a packet switched architecture can accommodate the scenarios outlined. These can easily be adapted based on operator’s individual requirements.

ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 3. In the above example, each CSR is connected using a single Ethernet link across dark fibre to the HSR. Other underlay transport technologies and topologies are available, such as redundant hub and spoke, chain or ring topologies in the access network. Regardless of the WAN technology and topology employed, careful consideration needs to be given the latency and jitter requirements of C/U plane traffic between the O-RU and the O-DU. Transport considerations includes fibre distances between the O-RU and the O-DU, the number of routers/switches traversed, link speeds and switching times of the intermediate transport network equipment. (see section 10.1.1.2 for more details). As O-RAN 7.2x traffic loads are dependent on user activity and in the example there are multiple O-RUs in the cell site, the link capacity between the CSR and HSR does not need to be provisioned at the theoretical sum of the O-RU’s peak rates because a statistical gain can be realised. The bandwidth provisioning should be based on usage and the real achievable peak rates associated with the O-RUs. The real achievable peak rates are dependent on factors such as number and proximity of radios to each other and environmental factors. Precise provisioning rules for 5G Fronthaul is subject to further investigation.

# 17 20.4.1.3 QoS
1. The QoS scheme outlined in section 20.2.1, Figure 20-4 will be applied across the transport network and is capable of supporting Fronthaul, Midhaul and Backhaul traffic running on the same link. O-RU and O-DU set appropriate QoS markings for C/U and M-plane traffic that transport network can trust. 3. In the above example, the C/U and M-plane traffic share the same physical interface, separated using VLANs between the O-RU and CSR and between HSR and O-DU. In this situation the mobile components (O-RUs and O-DUs) will need to support: o An internal scheduling mechanism to prioritise C/U plane traffic over M-Plane traffic onto the Ethernet interface o Depending on O-RU→ CSR and HSR→ O-DU link speeds, the O-RU, O-DU, CSR and HSR may need to support TSN frame pre-emption to control serialization delay. (refer to section 10.1.1.2.1 for more details). Alternatively, if the O-RU or CSR do not support TSN frame pre-emption or the O-DU or HSR do not support TSN frame pre-emption, then separate physical interfaces could be used to separate the C/U plane and M-plane traffic. 5. C/U and M-plane traffic from all O-RUs in the cell site share the same transport link between the CSR and the HSR. In most scenarios where a CSR supports multiple radios running fronthaul, this link will be 25Gbps or above and therefore does not really benefit from TSN frame pre-emption. However, in some instances, the link between the CSR and HSR may be lower speed and would benefit from TSN frame pre-emption. (see section

# 40 10.1.1.2.1 for more details)
6. C/U plane traffic must be prioritized over M-plane traffic on the WAN links. CSR and HSR must be provisioned at both the link level and within the link level queuing infrastructure in a manner such that C/U plane traffic is not dropped or experiences queuing delay in either the CSR or HSR (or any additional Transport Network Equipment in the path between the O-RU and the O-DU). M-plane traffic can experience a level of delay, so be configured to use a lower priority queue or a queuing scheme such as Weighted Round Robin that reserves a small amount of bandwidth for management traffic (see section 14 for an example) ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 4 Segment Routing architectural principle
There is a single SR architecture which is defined in RFC8402 [139]. This defines the general concepts of SR and is independent from the specific data plane. Currently, there are two instantiations of the SR architecture designed and implemented in production code, SR over MPLS

# 8 (SR-MPLS) and SR over IPv6 (SRv6).
The architecture relies on segments identifiers (SIDs) and SID lists. The SID represents a single instruction which can be related to how the packet is forwarded or a function that needs to be performed on a packet. A SID lists or the SR policy is a collection of SIDs or instructions to be performed on the packet as it traverses the SR domain. Typically, a SID list is imposed on the packets as it enters the SR domain and is either empty or completed by the time it leaves an SR domain. There are two basic types of segment, global segments which correspond to instructions that are globally valid in an SR domain and local segments which correspond to instructions that are only valid within a single node. Some of the key segment types are: 1. IGP Prefix and IGP node segments: These are global SIDs and are instructions on how to forward a packet towards a destination IP network or destination IP node. As the name suggests these are conveyed by IGP and can be used by any node in the SR domain to send traffic to a node or IP prefix. 2. Adjacency segments: These are local SIDs which identify the links available on that node. 3. Anycast segments: These are a special IGP-prefix segment that corresponds to an anycast prefix. ie a prefix advertised by more than one router. Anycast and anycast segments are commonly used to provide high availability or load balancing solutions. 4. Binding Segments: These are a single SID that is associated with a segment list or SR policy. This means the node that processes the Binding SID replaces the single segment with a segment list. Using Figure 21-1 as an example, the basic SR architecture can support: 1. A dynamically locally computed forwarding path between an ingress and egress point within the SR domain by the ingress node either imposing the node SID of the egress node or the prefix SID of the destination prefix. Typically, a link-state IGP or an EGP routing protocol, running locally on the routers calculate these types of paths and they exhibit the behaviour of normal routing protocols such “Shortest Path Forwarding” and “Equal Cost

# 37 Multi Pathing (ECMP)
2. A fully deterministic path between the ingress and egress points. In this case the SR policy or SID list includes all nodes on the path and if required adjacency SIDs to select links between nodes. 3. A combination of the two. The SR architecture can build a path between an ingress and egress node that combines dynamically computed forwarding and explicitly routed forwarding. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 3 IPv6 (SRv6).

# 4 SR-MPLS
The MPLS data plane (SR-MPLS) is specified in RFC 8660 “Segment Routing with MPLS data plane”[146], In the case of SR-MPLS, Segment Routing does not require any change to the MPLS forwarding plane. An SR Policy is instantiated through the MPLS Label Stack and the Segment IDs (SIDs) of a Segment List are inserted as MPLS Labels. The classical forwarding functions available for MPLS networks allow implementing the SR operations.

# 10 IPv6 data plane (SRv6)
For the IPv6 data plane (SRv6), a new type of IPv6 Routing Extension Header, called Segment Routing Header (SRH) has been defined in RFC 8754 IPv6 Segment Routing Header (SRH) [151]. The SRH contains the Segment List (SR Policy) as an ordered list of IPv6 addresses: each address in the list is a SID. A dedicated field, referred to as Segments Left, is used to maintain the pointer to the active SID of the Segment List. This SRH format and basic operation of the SRH is illustrated in Figure 21-2. Figure 21-2 SRH header and interaction between segments left and SID list To explain the SRv6 data plane, there are three categories of nodes: Source SR nodes, Transit nodes and SR Segment Endpoint nodes. A Source SR node corresponds to the headend node, it can be a host originating an IPv6 packet, or an SR domain ingress router encapsulating a received packet in an outer IPv6 header. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 Figure 21-3 Packet and SRH construct for IPv4 payload for traffic following nodes 1,2,5 In Figure 21-3, which considers the latter case the source SR node (S1) is an edge router that encapsulates a packet (which can be IPv6, IPv4 or an Layer 2 frame) into an outer IPv6 packet and inserts the SR Header (SRH) as a Routing Extension Header in the outer IPv6 header. The traffic is destined for S5 and for policy reasons the operator wishes to send the traffic via S2 and S3 which is not the shortest IGP path. To implement this policy, a segment list is composed of S2 and S5. S3 does not need to be specified because the shortest path from S2 to S5 is via S3. To implement this SR policy and assuming the use of a reduced SRH (for details see RFC8754[146]) the packet details are shown in Figure 21-3. In addition to the basic operations, the SRv6 Network Programming model [154] describes a set of functions that can be associated to segments and executed in a given SRv6 node. Examples of such functions are: different types of packet encapsulation (e.g. IPv6 in IPv6, IPv4 in IPv6, Ethernet in IPv6), corresponding decapsulation, lookup operation on a specific routing table (e.g. to support VPNs). The list of functions described in [154] is not meant to be exhaustive, as any function can be associated to a segment identifier in a node. Obviously, the definition of a standardized set of segment routing functions facilitates the deployment of SR domains with interoperable equipment from multiple vendors.

# 21 Segment Routing control plane
The control plane is responsible for calculating, building the connectivity graphs and implementing the SR policies within the network. Segment Routing can support distributed, centralised or hybrid control plane architectures. See Figure 21-4 for more details. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 17 MPLS-SR distributed control plane
The MPLS-SR distributed control plane utilises ISIS or OSPF routing protocols with extensions to advertise the different types of IGP segments (prefix, node, adjacency, any cast) between TNEs.

# 21 IPv6 distributed control plane
For the IPv6 data plane, the process of advertising the IGP-prefix, IGP-node and IGP-anycast segments is simplified due to the use of IPv6 addresses as SIDs. In particular, there is no need to extend the IGP routing protocols to distribute these segment types, because they are IPv6 prefixes natively distributed by the routing protocols. This means that the Control Plane for SRv6 can use the regular IPv6 link state IGP routing protocols (OSPFv3, ISIS) to support the basic operations, while extensions are still needed ([149][150]) to distribute IGP-Adjacency segments and other SR configuration information.

# 29 Centralised control plane
Although much emphasis has been made of fully centralised control plane models in academia for path computation, they have not made their ways into production large scale WAN designs due to the distributed nature of the transport nodes and the need for the transport nodes to communicate at ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 all times with the central controller. As a consequence, most WAN SDN designs today are hybrid in nature, where intelligence is split between the TNEs and central SDN controllers. Note: This discussion above only considers path computation element of a central controller. There are many aspects of a central SDN controller including orchestration, data analytics etc.

# 6 Hybrid control plane
The hybrid control plane is combination of distributed control plane and centralised SDN control plane functionality. Like the central control plane model there is no universal architecture for a hybrid control plane design, other than some functions are provided centrally and others occur locally on the TNEs. One of the most common hybrid control plane designs is where the central SDN controllers provides a “Path Computation Element” capability. In this model the PCE is responsible for path computation and inter-domain routing with the distributed control planes running on the TNEs, responsible for building the link state database, calculating the network graph and building the shortest path forwarding tables. In this scenario there is generally a tight relationship between the two components. A. The TNEs exchange topology information, creates the link-state database and computes the shortest path forwarding tables. B. The centralised control plane component needs to get visibility of the distributed protocol’s link-state database to understand the current topology. Some of the common approaches are: a. The SDN controller participates in the IGP and as a consequence builds its own link- state database and network graph. b. The SDN controller extracts IGP databases from the network using proprietary mechanisms. c. BGP-LS (BGP link state) runs between one or more TNEs and centralised controllers. In this way the centralised controller gets visibility of the network through BGP-LS. C. In many instances the centralised control plane needs to gather other information about the network, for example link loading. Currently, there is no single standard for collecting this information. Common mechanisms include SNMP, telemetry feeds and operational data from

# 31 Yang models residing on the devices.
D. The central controller and the TNEs also need to communicate when, either a TNE requests a service from the central SDN controller, or the central SDN controller wants to push an explicit policy to a TNE. An example would be if a TNE needs build an SR policy and wants to use the services of a PCE. The transport node and the PCE need to communicate, some of the common protocols used for this type of communications include: a. Network Configuration Protocol b. PCE (PCEP) c. BGP d. Openflow (SR-MPLS)

# 9 EVPN E-LAN service
EVPN E-LAN service is a Layer 2 multipoint-to-multipoint service. In essence, EVPN E-LAN emulates Layer 2 switch behavior, with attachment circuits (ACs) of this single emulated Layer 2 switch present on multiple Provider Edge (PE) routers, which are placed in different network locations, as outlined in Figure 22-1 CE1 PE1 PE3 CE3 BGP BGP BGP CE2 BGP PE4 PE2 CE4 CE1 CE3 CE2 CE4

# 9 EVPN E-Tree service
EVPN E-Tree service is an enhancement of EVPN E-LAN service, which allows to restrict certain communication patterns, creating in essence a point-to-multipoint service model. As outlined in Figure 22-2, each attachment circuit is designated as root (R) or leaf (L). As per EVPN E-Tree definition, only rootroot and rootleaf Layer 2 communication is permitted, while leafleaf

# 14 Layer 2 communication is blocked.
BGP BGP

# 16 Figure 22-2 EVPN E-Tree services
At a high level, EVPN E-LAN service can be considered as a special case of EVPN E-Tree service, with all attachment circuits designated as root. In fact, many vendors use the same configuration constructs for EVPN E-LAN and EVPN E-Tree, defaulting the attachment circuit to a root, with some configuration knobs turning it to a leaf.

# 22 EVPN E-Line service
EVN E-Line, called as well EVPN Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS), is point-to-point Layer 2 service, without MAC learning. Ethernet frame received from an end device connected via single- homed or multi-homed attachment circuit, is transported over this point-to-point service to the remote end device, connected again via single-homed or multi-homed attachment circuit. Since it is pure point-to-point communication, no MAC learning is required, and thus MAC learning is not part of EVPN E-Line (VPWS) architecture.

# 8 EVPN VLAN-bundle service
The biggest challenge with basic EVPN VLAN-based service is scaling. In EVPN VLAN-based service each VLAN consumes dedicated EVI, thus the maximum numbers of VLANs that can be served is limited by the supported EVIs on given hardware platform. EVPN VLAN-bundle service addresses this scaling limitation by bundling multiple VLANs into single bridge (MAC learning) domain/table and single EVI (MAC-VRF), as outlined in Figure 22-5

# 16 Figure 22-5 EVPN VLAN-bundle service (E-LAN, E-Tree, E-Line)
ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 VLAN bundling allows dramatic reduction of MAC-VRFs that otherwise would be needed on the router. Therefore, EVPN VLAN-bundle service is typically used in high-scale environment, with large number of VLANs or VLAN combination (QinQ) that must be transported with EVPN service. This scaling improvements brings improvements, as well some restrictions for service deployment, namely:
- the original VLAN tag must be carried with frame across EVPN network and VLAN
translation is not supported

# 10 • MACs cannot be re-used across different VLANs
The first restriction is related to the fact, that underlying transport identification (i.e. MPLS label with MPLS underlay transport, Function:Argument with SRv6 underlay transport) identifies the bridge domain. Therefore, the underlying transport identification cannot be used to distinguish Ethernet frames - received over EVPN network - as belonging to different VLANs, if VLAN tag is stripped before sending Ethernet frames across EVPN. And this differentiation is required to maintain per-VLAN broadcast/flooding restrictions. Second restriction is the straight result of bundling multiple VLANs in single bridge (MAC learning) domain/table. All these bundled VLANs use the same MAC table, therefore all MACs must be unique across all bundle VLANs.

# 22 EVPN VLAN-aware bundle Service
Restrictions of EVPN VLAN-bundle services are removed by EVPN VLAN-aware bundle service. EVPN VLAN-aware bundle service is a trade-off between EVPN VLAN-based service (poor scaling, but simple service without restrictions related to VLAN translation or MAC learning) and EVPN VLAN-bundle service (good scaling, but restricting VLAN translation support and requiring

# 27 MAC uniqueness).

# 30 Why do we need QoS?
Applications using the network transport will often require certain capabilities from the network in order for the application to function correctly. For example, real-time voice services (telephone calls) can only sustain a maximum latency between the end points before interactive speech becomes difficult. This maximum latency between endpoints translates to two demands from the network; 1. Minimising hop by hop latency as a voice packet flows across the network infrastructure. 2. Minimising jitter in the packets arriving in order to minimise the de-jitter buffer needed at the receiver (which adds latency). It is useful then to be able to identify voice traffic in the network and prioritise if for forwarding such that it is not held up behind other less time sensitive traffic. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 A second example might be an Electronic Point of Sale (EPoS) application. This type of application does not need to be particularly latency bound (a few 10s or 100s of milliseconds in packet arrival does not impact the service), but it does need to have some guaranteed capacity in order to function. I.e. we do not want the EPoS application struggling for bandwidth because a large data transfer is taking place. This guaranteed bandwidth requirement also translates into network demands. 1. Minimising packet loss for the traffic, if necessary, storing it locally until the local egress interface has capacity to send it on. 2. Reserving a minimum amount of transmission time (or bandwidth) on the interface for packets of the EPoS application. QoS then is the mechanism by which operators can identify applications in an infrastructure and apply policies to the infrastructure to maintain the applications transport requirements, even when capacity is limited. QoS functional elements As a suite of capabilities QoS can be broken out into three distinct sets of functions;

# 18 1. Traffic Classification and marking

# 19 2. Congestion avoidance

# 20 3. Congestion management
These three function sets work together to identify (classify) different traffic types, determine how much of each traffic type should be allowed into and through the network (congestion avoidance) and how traffic should be scheduled when interfaces become congested (congestion management). The specific implementation of these capabilities is vendor specific, but in general, the behaviours required by the different functions are defined as policies, either individually or in groups. These policies are applied to interfaces on the switching elements in a network defining the local behaviours within the device. Network level behaviour QoS is implicitly a mechanism that is node based; the management of traffic in one node has no direct impact on the management of traffic in surrounding nodes. However, it is important to design the QoS behaviour of a network as a whole. Just as the operator has the ability to define the routing behaviour of a network as a system of single hop by hop elements, so she has the ability to define the QoS behaviour of the network as a system. The interaction between elements is defined by the policies applied to each device and the use of “class of service” markings applied to the packets or frames flowing between the devices. 1 The use of markings allows an individual network element to pass some information about a given packet to a downstream element. How this downstream element interprets the information and then The term “class of service” is used here to generically to describe the specific markings in a packet or frame. The author recognises Class of Service (COS) identifies such markings in an ethernet header as defined by IEEE 802.1p. Here it is generically used to refer to Ethernet COS, IP TOS, IP PREC, IP DSCP. MPLS EXP etc. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 acts on it, is out of the upstream elements control, but a network of devices under single administrative control may choose to use such information in network wide policy. Node level behaviour

# 7 Figure 24-1: Example network QoS structure
The per-hop-behaviours (PHBs) needed in the network can generally be broken down into two sets; Those needed at the edge of the network (Edge QoS), and those needed in the core of the network (Core QoS). We can see these behaviours in Figure 24-1. 1. Edge QoS. Here we are classifying traffic entering into the network on ingress (1) and scheduling traffic leaving the network on egress (6). Here the ingress classification (from the client) and egress classification (5) and scheduling (6) (towards the client) will (often) be determined by the markings of the client traffic being transported across the network. In addition, ingress traffic (CE → PE), once classified, will be marked (2) to conform to the transport marking scheme. 2. Core QoS. Here traffic will be classified by the transport marking scheme (4) (mentioned above), scheduled based on those markings (3). This PHB is designed to manage traffic at an aggregate level, treating services that have common requirements (defined by marking) with a common behaviour. These two sets of PHBs present different requirements to the underlying hardware and care should be taken when selecting a platform to ensure the operators desired PHBs can be met.

# 29 Traffic classification and marking
As previously mentioned, traffic classification is a term used to describe the identification and categorisation of traffic arriving at or inside network element. Classification broadly falls into two distinct categories. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 10 Figure 24-2: Context based classification
In a second example, all traffic arriving on a specific interface might be classified (categorised) as

# 13 “real time” or “high priority” (see Figure 24-2).
Whilst use of context-based classification is important, it is a somewhat blunt tool, and assumes that all traffic arriving on an interface is of a single type and requires common treatment.

# 17 Packet based classification
Packet based classification gives us a more selective tool with which to categorize traffic arriving at a node. In this mode the node examines one or more fields in the arriving packets (or frames) to make a categorisation decision. One approach is to classify traffic into categories based on some flow or application information. E.g. looking at source or destination, ether type, IP protocol, UDP or TCP port number etc. In this way the node can infer the required QoS capabilities (e.g. low latency, minimum bandwidth, best effort etc) from the type of traffic embedded in the packet. However, often the most pragmatic approach is to require that packets are pre-marked with an explicit class of service marking. The specific marking model varies dependent on the transport being used, but the primary marking schemes to support are Ethernet Priority Code Point (PCP) and Drop Eligible Indicator (DEI) fields in Ethernet IEEE 802.1p (part of the IEEE 802.1q VLAN header specification), IP TOS, PREC or DSCP ECN fields (defined in IETF RFC 2474 [49] and RFC 3168) and MPLS TC (EXP) field (defined in IEFT RFC 3032 [61] and RFC 5462). The use of a class of service (COS) marking allows a packet source or network element to encode the required QOS capabilities for a packet directly into the packet header. By predetermining the marking scheme to be used for the COS field, classification using the COS field alone is often sufficient to determine the PHB needed in the network node. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 24 Figure 24-3: QoS marking domains
A useful concept is to consider the use of a given marking scheme within a QoS marking domain. Nodes within a domain use a common scheme, allowing identification of traffic with common properties (a traffic class). Policies are then implemented in each node to maintain the appropriate network behaviour for each identified class, when under congested conditions. At the border between domains, the border element should be capable of classifying traffic in the first domain and remarking it for transport in the second. Usually the policy for forwarding will be implemented to honour the class structure for the domain it is in. In Figure 24-3, three domains are identified, 1) the customer domain, 2) the provider domain 3) an intra-node domain. The PE ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 elements on the left and right of the provider domain border the provider and customer domains and will be responsible for remarking traffic as appropriate.

# 4 Congestion management
Thus far we have discussed the options available for classifying traffic. But once classified, we must consider what behaviour to apply. As mentioned in the introduction to this section, a QoS node fundamentally only has three options available for managing traffic; forward, store for forwarding later or drop, but these options need only be applied when a bandwidth resource is congested. A key function of QoS is that of managing traffic during congestion of an interface. Congestion occurs when the quantity of traffic to be forwarded on an interface exceeds its capacity. In its simplest form, QoS alleviates this issue by buffering the excess traffic, i.e. storing it in a local memory until such time that the interface is available to send the stored traffic.

# 16 FIFO Queueing
By storing packets that need to be sent on to this interface in the order they arrive, and then sending them in that order when the interface is free, we form a “first in - first out” (FIFO) queue of packets. This mechanism, queueing, is a useful tool for managing temporary congestion, smoothing out the bursts of traffic flowing into an interface, and forms the basis for more complex congestion management tools. There are four aspects of this capability that cause challenges; 1. By storing traffic for later sending, we intrinsically delay that traffic that is being stored, adding latency to the transmission path for that traffic. Further, because the delay may be variable, (different amounts of traffic may be enqueued prior to this packet arriving) we introduce jitter. 2. As the speeds of the interfaces we are managing increases, we need more memory capacity to store enough packets to substantively impact the traffic we are buffering. 3. The process is of queuing traffic is indiscriminate, in that it impacts all traffic flowing through an interface. This presents the same latency implication to all applications using this interface, some of which will be impacted by this delay, and some will not. 4. As the amount of memory available to for the queue is finite, so the queue is finite. As a result, if the rate of arrival of traffic to be forwarded is significantly higher than the interface rate or the burst is long enough, the available buffer will be filled, and no further traffic can be enqueued. At this point, the node has no option but to drop traffic. When a queue is full, and a node can no longer add packets to the end (tail) of the queue, traffic otherwise destined for that queue is indiscriminately dropped from the tail (tail drop), until such time that the queue depth reduces and space is made available again for new traffic. It is worth remembering at this point that the application of QoS to an infrastructure is only a solution for the management of how traffic is dropped under congestion conditions. It is not a replacement for capacity planning and management for traffic that MUST be delivered. I.e. if a network has less capacity available than the amount of traffic that MUST be delivered, applying QoS is not an alternative to augmenting the capacity. However, it is possible to significantly improve on this single FIFO queue model by combining the use of classification with a programable scheduler to determine how we enqueue traffic, how much we allow to pass, and what to do with the excess. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 8 Figure 24-4: Class based queue
In this model, shown in Figure 24-4, the system identifies separate logical queues for traffic destined to flow out of a given interface. Traffic can be placed into a queue based on the classification information gained on arrival (or if the system is capable, after the packet has been forwarded – determined that it should flow out of this specific interface). For example, traffic identified as needing low latency, and low jitter (real time – our voice calls from earlier) may be placed into queue 1. Traffic requiring some minimum bandwidth (business critical, our EPOS traffic) may be placed into queue 3. Traffic that has no specific requirements

# 18 (best effort) may be placed into queue 5.
The scheduler can now be programmed to dequeue traffic and place it onto the interface following a pre-determined policy – for example; 1. Serve all high-priority traffic first (E.g. Queue 1 and 2), up to a given capacity of the interface for each queue (for example 50% and 5%). Any traffic arriving at this interface for those queues that cannot be served at that rate should be placed into the appropriate queue. 2. Serve traffic from low priority queues (queue 3, 4 and 5) with equal priority (a packet from each) until the minimum guaranteed amount of bandwidth allocated to that queue is met. 3. Continue to serve traffic from low priority queues until either the queue is empty, or the interface bandwidth is consumed. This type of policy allows maximum use of the available bandwidth whilst guaranteeing each application class will have access to at least the capacity it needs to support the user base.

# 33 Hierarchical class-based queueing
A further extension of this model uses a tiered set of schedulers to manage sets of queues that are “grouped” to manage traffic associated with some logical entity on the physical interface. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 3 Figure 24-5: Hierarchical class-based queue model
In Figure 24-5, we have a physical interface supporting two VLANs (orange and green). Each VLAN has its own set of queues and its own scheduling policy for those queues. In this example the orange VLAN has two priority queues and three guaranteed bandwidth queues. The top scheduler (2) is responsible for managing the flow of traffic from the queues associated with that VLAN. The bottom scheduler (3) manages this flow of traffic from the queue associated with the green

# 10 VLAN.
Schedulers (2) and (3) are regarded as child schedulers, and their packet flow is in turn managed by scheduler (1), the parent scheduler for the interface. The parent scheduler will be programmed with a policy to manage the traffic flowing from the child schedulers toward the interface. This model can allow for a “hard” distribution of the bandwidth on an interface amongst the logic entities sharing that capacity, protecting the use of the bandwidth for a given VLAN (orange) from the others on the same interface (green).

# 19 Congestion avoidance
Thus far we have discussed the options available for classifying traffic, and managing traffic when interfaces are under congestion. We have examined how, when an interface is congested, we can consider which packets to forward and when. However, one important aspect of QoS is the prevention of congestion in the first place.

# 25 Congestion avoidance predominantly takes two forms;

# 26 1. Admission control
2. Selective queue management through random early discard (RED) or weighted random early discard (WRED) ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 12 Figure 24-6: Admission control policing
By pre-agreeing that the network can only sustain a certain number of calls, we can police the traffic arriving from the application, to the agreed level. In the case of the packet network, this means agreeing a sustainable bandwidth level and honouring that level at the point that we accept traffic from the application. Once we have classified traffic to determine that it is indeed voice traffic, we can apply a policer to that traffic class to limit the amount of traffic that is accepted. If the application violates the agreed rate, the policer will drop some packets, forwarding only the rate that was previously agreed. It should be noted that for this particular application, again voice quality will suffer, however, the onus is now on the application to stay within the terms of the agreed contract for the benefit of its own service. So, if by dropping traffic at admission to the network we will see the application service degrade, just as if we drop traffic in the middle of the network, why bother? Should we not simply let the traffic have access and hope there is sufficient capacity to support the application demand? ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 3 Figure 24-7: Service protection through admission control
This is where the network level administration of QoS becomes relevant. Consider the same core network resource now being shared by two customers (Figure 24-7). If we recognise that the network can only sustain 100 calls, we can ask each customer to restrict their usage, customer 1 to 60 calls and customer 2 to 40 calls. By applying a policy that is specific to each customer context we can ensure that the available network resources are not exhausted, resulting in poor performance for all. If customer 1 exceeds their allocated capacity, some traffic will be dropped at point 1, resulting in poor quality for customer 1. However, if customer 2 continues to maintain their agreement not to exceed 40 calls, there will always be sufficient capacity to support their service without quality impairment.

# 16 Weighted Random Early Discard (WRED)
When looking at congestion management, the idea of a queue was introduced in order to store traffic that is awaiting transmission on an outgoing interface. In this previous discussion we saw that in a simple queue, when the queue is full, any additional traffic is “tail dropped” indiscriminately. For applications that are using a TCP connection over IP, the loss of one (or more) packets from the flow will cause the TCP algorithm to time out and request re-delivery of these missing packets. This also triggers the shortening of the TCP “ack window” resulting in lower throughput for that TCP session. As many TCP session may be impacted at once in a tail drop scenario, this can cause a number of sessions to “back off” reducing the total load on the interface, and the queue to be drained. Over time, the TCP sessions will re-open their ACK window, increasing bandwidth until the interface is once again full and the queue overwhelmed. The result is a sawtooth type bandwidth profile that oscillates around the maximum interface speed. This oscillation reduces the efficiency of the interface usage as there are periods where the interface is not full. Weighted Random early discard (WRED) is a modification to the queue drop behaviour that can help to eliminate this effect. The premise is to manage the acceptance of traffic into the queue in a more intelligent manner. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 19 Class based Weighted Random Early Discard
We have seen it is possible to add traffic to a specific queue based on a classification, in order to differentiate between traffic types flowing in an interface. This allows us the flexibility to manage bandwidth to support different applications in an infrastructure. We have also seen that under some circumstances it might be possible to “borrow” bandwidth from one class to use in another class, in the event that the bandwidth in an interface is not fully used. It is possible to extend the idea differentiated behaviour for traffic from between queues, to within a single queue using the Weighted RED scheme.

# 29 Figure 24-9: Class based WRED function and behaviour
Consider the PE node on the left of Figure 24-9, two CEs are sending EPOS traffic. The PE has capacity at (3) for 100 concurrent sessions. The number of sessions sent by each CE varies. CE 1 ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 has a minimum sustained rate of 60 sessions, and CE 2 has a minimum sustained rate of 40. Each has a possible peak rate of 100. As traffic arrives from CE 1 at point (1) the PE node classifies traffic as part of the EPOS application. It also measures the amount arriving and allows up to 100 sessions worth into the network. For traffic that exceeds the rate of 60 sessions, the node marks this traffic as having exceeded its contracted rate or “out of contract”. The same classification, policing and marking takes place at point (2) for CE 2 with a rate of 40 sessions. This extra marking is termed the discard class or DC. When the incoming packets arrive at the queue depicted on the right, again a decision is made prior to enqueuing the traffic. This time the decision is based on two criteria, the current queue depth AND the discard class of the packet as determined in the ingress policing and marking stages. A sample policy may behave as follows. For queue depth between 0% (4) and 33% (5) all traffic is enqueued. For traffic that is marked with the out-of-contract discard class marking, between queue depth 33% (5) and 66% (6) the drop probability varies from 0 to 1; that is at depth 66% (6) all traffic that is marked out of contract will be dropped. Traffic that is marked “in contract” will continue to be queued for transmission. For queue depths between 66% (6) and 100% (7) no out of contract traffic will be enqueued, and the drop probability for in contract traffic will increase from 0 to 1. It should be noted that the PE is not policing “sessions”, but simply the traffic associated with those sessions. The PE has no knowledge of the nature of the traffic sent by the CE (for example the membership of a specific packet to a specific session), other than the markings being examined. It should also be noted that traffic dropped at point (3) will contain packets associated with many or all of the sessions from the CE whose traffic is being marked “out-of-contract”. The impact of this is that all TCP sessions that lose traffic will again contract their TCP windows, with the effect of lowering the BW used by each session and so reducing the load on the network.

# 34 This behaviour has the following benefits;
1. both CE users 1 and 2 potentially have access to all the bandwidth at point 3 in the diagram when the other user is not consuming it. The network resources at 3 can be optimally used when demand from one user is high and the other is low. Compare this to the example in Service protection through admission control where the network resource at point 3 may be under used. 2. If a user constrains their traffic to within the contracted limit, they are guaranteed delivery, even under congestion caused by out-of-contract traffic being generated by other users. ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00

# 20 PIM-based overlay signalling for IPVPN
The most straightforward way is to emulate a per-VPN pseudo LAN over the underlay network. The pseudo LAN is instantiated by a multicast GRE tunnel for the VPN. Every PE for the VPN joins that tunnel and can send both control plane (PIM messages) and data plane traffic over the tunnel. For example, multicast group 225.1.1.1 used for VPN1, 225.1.1.2 for VPN2, etc. This is referred to as PIM-MVPN and also commonly as Rosen-MVPN. It is documented in the historic RFC6037 and further in RFC6513 [119] (which documents both PIM- and BGP-based overlay signaling). Essentially, a PE runs PIM sessions over each pseudo LAN for each VPN. This is different from unicast, with which no per-VPN session is used. When there are a large number of VPNs, many PIM sessions and signalling (including message refreshes) are incurred so it does not scale well. Most implementations and deployments of PIM/Rosen-MVPN only use IP multicast tunnel in the underlay to emulate the pseudo LANs.

# 36 BGP-based overlay signalling for IPVPN and EVPN
For BGP-based signalling, the overlay signalling is done by BGP just like unicast case. It is referred to as C-multicast signalling (C for Customer) in RFC6513 [119]. BGP-based signaling use unified methods for both unicast and multicast, and inherits all BGP scaling mechanisms and properties. Multicast (IP) VPN with BGP based overlay signalling is referred to BGP-MVPN. While RFC6513[119] covers both PIM-MVPN and BGP-MVPN concepts, BGP-MVPN specific encoding and procedures are specified in RFC6514 [120] . ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 BGP-MVPN also defines mechanisms to signal what type and instance of provider/underlay tunnels are used to transport overlay multicast traffic over the underlay, via Inclusive or Selective PMSI Auto-Discovery routes (often referred to as I/S-PMSI or x-PMSI routes). IP multicast, RSVP-TE P2MP, mLDP P2MP/MP2MP, Ingress Replication, BIER and future additions could all be used as underlay tunnels. EVPN BUM (Broadcast, Unknown unicast and Multicast) only uses BGP overlay signalling and is modelled after BGP-MVPN. It is specified in RFC7432 [121] and further in RFC9572 [166]. BGP-MVPN and EVPN BUM have been widely deployed and are often referred to as Next

# 11 Generation MVPN (NG-MVPN).
Underlay multicast As mentioned above, overlay multicast traffic is transported via underlay multicast tunnels. Many tunnel types have been mature and widely deployed, but with Segment Routing and central control being widely adopted, it is necessary to review the pros and cons of various multicast technologies and see what is the best solution in the SR era. Traditionally, multicast requires per-tree state on all routers of a tree for efficient replication. PIM, RSVP-TE P2MP, mLDP P2MP/MP2MP are all signaling protocols to instantiate tree state on those routers, either from the tree leaves towards the tree root or vice versa. The new SR-P2MP (aka tree- sid) tunnels also requires per-tree state on all root/leaf and replication nodes, except that the signalling is directly from a central controller who also calculates the tree. Obviously, this does not go well with one principal of Segment Routing – no per-flow state inside the network. An alternative is Ingress Replication – the root tunnels individual copies directly to leaves so no per-tree state is needed inside the network. Since replication is done at the root, it is not efficient and does not work well for high fan-out hight data rate cases. BIER (RFC8279 [132], RFC8296 [134]) is a new technology that achieves efficient replication w/o incurring per-tree state, so it is the ideal multicast solution for an SR network. However, it uses a new encapsulation and forwarding algorithm, so it requires new hardware. While this makes it difficult to deploy in non-greenfield networks, there are very well-designed brownfield deployment methods, and all major vendors have BIER implementation & hardware available/upcoming. For an SR network, an operator may prefer to remove all legacy multicast signaling – PIM/RSVP/mLDP and switch to controller-based tree calculation and signaling via either PCEP or

# 37 BGP (i.e., SR-P2MP [draft-ietf-pim-sr-p2mp-policy[173]] [draft-ietf-spring-sr-replication-segment]
or BGP-signaled IP/MPLS multicast [draft-ietf-bess-bgp-multicast-controller[160]]). Notice that this still incurs per-tree state inside the network and the only real benefit is the central calculation of the tree based on many TE constraints/considerations. In summary, depending on many factors, multicast technologies can be considered in the following preference order: 1. PIM or mLDP/RSVP-TE P2MP that are already deployed in existing network

# 46 2. Controller calculated/signalled IP multicast or mLDP/RSVP/SR-P2MP tunnel
3. BIER if enough routers in the network support it ORAN-WG9.XPSAAS.0-R003-v09.00 MVPN/EVPN and Seamless MPLS/SR Given the vast scale of the transport network, a seamless architecture is used as described previously. In this architecture, two aspects have impacts to multicast: a) Only border routes have routes to edges nodes (that connect to 5G NFs like RAN/UPF), while internal routers only have routes to the border routes. b) Different ASes/areas may support/prefer different types of underlay tunnels For a), to establish end-to-end underlay tunnels across those different ASes/areas, PIM RPF vector [RFC5496][109] or mLDP Recursive FEC [RFC6512][118] can be used – a leaf router looks up the route to the tree root, with the BGP protocol nexthop being a border router in the local area/AS. It then encodes that border router’s address in PIM/mLDP signaling so that internal routers will signal towards that border router instead of the original root. When that border router gets the signaling, it encodes the next border router’s address so that the internal routers in the next AS/area will signal towards the next border router, and so on so forth. An alternative solution for a) is use controller signaled multicast, since the routers become dumb forwarding devices programed with forwarding state for the tunnels by the controllers. For b), MVPN/EVPN-BUM tunnel segmentation RFC7524 [123] and draft-ietf-bess-bgp-multicast- controller [168] can be used – MVPN/EVPN-BUM procedures will run on the border routers and the signaled tunnel type/identification are changed as MVPN/EVPN routes are re-advertised by the border routers, so that different tunnel types/instances are used in different ASes/areas.

Underlay network for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 A packet switched network has extensive capabilities to support slicing. These are outlined in section 18. Slicing phase 1 is basic in nature with limited slicing capabilities in the O-RAN mobile components and the actual slices (mobile BB, MMTc, NB-IOT) are low priority and delay tolerant slices. In phase 2, some additional slice types are added (MBB IPTV, Enterprise Core, Enterprise Private Cloud), with more distributed 3GPP, O-RAN component and Application Functions (UPFs and CDNs can be located at regional and central DC levels), and more – but still not very critical – delay sensitivity (for example IPTV). Phase 3 adds even distribution possibilities. With this in mind, and more onerous slicing use cases in later phases, it is proposed to support slicing phase 1 and 2 in the transport network using:
- Default IGP instances running in each underlay routing domain calculating shortest path
routing based on IGP metrics.

# 42 • IGP supporting fast and loop free convergence.
- Inter-domain connectivity performed using either BGP, IGP redistributing or a PCE
infrastructure.
- Management, control and user planes in phase 1 and 2 use shortest path routing between
TNEs. I.e., the Service VPNs associated with each slice are not mapped to TE tunnels or
